title: Europe
body: Europe is a continent that is between Asia and the Atlantic Ocean and is north of the Mediterranean Sea

title: estate

title: Pupils can struggle with the fact that the United Kingdom is a country made up of four separate smaller countries. Furthermore we also refer to Great Britain - which can again be confusing for pupils.
body: The UK's full name is The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland make up the UK. Great Britain is only the mainland countries of England, Wales and Scotland that share land borders.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Victorian childhood was very different to childhood today.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many Victorian children needed to work, both in towns and in the countryside.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a Victorian illustration, a child can be seen fainting in the fields due to the hard work.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Children worked in factories and mines, and as chimney sweeps; these jobs were often very dangerous.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historical sources show many children died or were injured doing these dangerous jobs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mines
body: mines are deep holes dug in the ground to find precious materials like coal or metal
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chimney sweep
body: someone who sweeps the soot out of chimneys is called a chimney sweep
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sources
body: sources are things from the past that historians look at to try and find out what life was like at that time
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may believe that all Victorian children worked, or that no Victorian children had an education.
body: Children from wealthy families were educated at home or sent to schools that were paid for. Some children went to small local schools on some days of the week and worked on other days. Some of the least fortunate children did not go to school at all.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Britain had an empire which meant it controlled a lot of places across the world, including countries in Africa.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Towards the end of Victoria's reign, a woman called Alice Kinloch travelled a long way to come to Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alice Kinloch was born in South Africa, and had come to Britain with an important mission.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She wanted to speak out about the poor conditions that African miners faced when they worked to find diamonds.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alice helped to set up a group of people to speak up and help the miners in South Africa.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: empire
body: an empire is a group of countries or provinces ruled from the centre by a person or group of people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: South Africa
body: South Africa is a country located in the southern part of the continent of Africa
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diamond
body: a diamond is a precious gemstone found deep under the earth's surface that has taken millions of years to form
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: miners
body: miners are people who work in mines, digging for coal, metals or precious stones like diamonds
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That 'South Africa' refers to the southern half of the continent of Africa.
body: 'South Africa' is one single African country, which is located in the south of the continent of Africa. The south of africa (the part that sits in the southern hemisphere) covers a much larger area and includes 15 other individual African countries.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During Victorian times, the British Empire controlled many countries around the world including India.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Britain had gradually taken control of more and more territory of India before and during Victoria's reign.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1876, Victoria was given the special title 'Empress of India'.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Later in Victoria's life, one of her most faithful servants was called Abdul Karim, who was from India.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of Victoria's other household servants were angered by Abdul and did not want to treat him as an equal.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: India
body: In this historical context, India refers to the British-controlled territories in South Asia during the period of British colonial rule, including Punjab, the Sikh Empire's homeland.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: empress
body: the female leader of an empire is called an empress
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: servants
body: a person who has a job working in someone else's home is a servant
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: household
body: a ruler's household includes all the people who support a ruler and live in the same building as them or very near to them
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that Britain still rules over or controls India today.
body: Britain does not rule India today. Britain ruled India and much of the surrounding land for over 300 years, but this ended in 1947 when the territory was partitioned into two separate independent countries which became India and Pakistan.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Queen Victoria died in 1901 having reigned for 63 years; only Elizabeth II reigned for longer.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By the time of Victoria's death, Britain had changed a great deal.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Britain's empire had continued to grow, with Britain controlling land across six of the world's continents.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Laws now protected children from working at a young age, and gave them the right to free education.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Laws had been passed to clean up dirty cities and to build new sewers and water supplies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: laws
body: laws are a set of rules that everyone has to follow
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: education
body: the way we learn about the world, gain new skills and prepare for the future through school, books or experiences
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That when Queen Victoria died, then Queen Elizabeth II became queen.
body: There were other monarchs in between Queen Victoria and Queen Elizabeth II. Queen Elizabeth II was the next female monarch but she did not become queen until 50 years after Queen Victoria died.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An awareness of what Britain was like towards the end of the nineteenth century, as introduced in 'Queen Victoria: how did Britain change during her lifetime?'
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An awareness of the behaviour of rulers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: On the 4th of June 1913, a tragedy occurred at Epsom Racecourse.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A woman called Emily Davison ran out onto the course during a big horse race called the Epsom Derby.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Emily ran out onto the course because she was fighting for a change to take place in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She was knocked over by the King's horse and died from her injuries.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tragedy
body: a play dealing with tragic events and often ends with a death
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vote
body: a vote gives people a choice as to who they want to represent them in the government
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that Emily Davison died on the day of the Epsom Derby.
body: Emily Davison died four days after the race at Epsom, on the 8th of June 1913.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Emily Davison was born in South East London in 1872.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When she was eight years old, one of her sisters died from a deadly disease, diphtheria.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Emily loved reading so much that she went on to study literature at university.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She did well in her studies and got such high marks that she should have received a degree.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, as a woman, Emily was not allowed to get a degree.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diphtheria
body: diphtheria was a common childhood disease in Victorian England which affected the throat or skin
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: literature
body: literature is writing that is thought of as a work of art
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: degree
body: a degree is a certificate to show someone has completed studying a subject at university
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that women were not allowed to go to university at all in Victorian Britain.
body: Women were allowed to study at university, work very hard and take all of the same exams as men, but they were not allowed the degree at the end of it.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Not getting her degree because she was a woman made Emily Davison very angry.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Something else that women were not allowed to do was to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This made Emily very angry as well.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Emily joined a group of women who were fighting for women to be allowed to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This group was called the Suffragettes.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vote
body: a vote gives people a choice as to who they want to represent them in the government
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Suffragettes
body: the Suffragettes were a group of people who wanted women to have the right to vote in Britain
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that Emily Davison quit her job to join the Suffragettes.
body: Emily joined the Suffragettes in 1906 and did not quit her job to fight for women's suffrage full time until 1908.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Suffragettes did lots of things to fight for women to be allowed to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were militant: prepared to break the law and go to prison to accomplish this.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Emily Davison was arrested lots of times for the things she did.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She broke windows, set fire to postboxes and even threw stones at an important politician.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In prison, Emily even stopped eating to try to show how important it was for women to be allowed to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: politician
body: a politician is a person who works in the government
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: militant
body: to be forceful, determined and extreme, sometimes using aggressive methods
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: arrested
body: when someone is arrested, they are taken away by the police because they have broken the law
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: law
body: a law is a rule that tells people what they can and cannot do
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some children might think that militant tactics are a good way for them to get the things that they want to.
body: The Suffragettes used extreme tactics because they felt that it was their only option. Going on hunger strike is dangerous. For the issues that children might face, there are many safer and less harmful ways to make a change.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some historians think Emily was trying to put a suffragette banner on a horse at the racecourse.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Others think that she was prepared to die so that women could get the vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Whatever her motives, Emily was recognised at the time for being very brave.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Suffragettes organised a large funeral procession; 5,000 of them marched in the streets of London with her coffin.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 50,000 people came out to watch her coffin moving through London and to pay respect.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: funeral
body: a funeral is an event where people come together to remember a person who has died
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pay respect
body: to pay respect to someone means to remember a person who has died
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: procession
body: a procession is a group of people moving forward together
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that thousands of people attend funerals usually.
body: Emily Davison's funeral was an exception. Usually funerals are only attended by people who knew the person.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The year after Emily Davison died, a large war broke out and men in Britain had to go and fight.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With the men gone, women had to take on their jobs; they showed how strong and capable they were.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the end of the war, people appreciated how much women had done while the men were away.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They also remembered how brave suffragettes like Emily Davison were.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As a result, it was decided that some women should be allowed to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: First World War
body: the First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918 and involved countries from all over the world, including Britain
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vote
body: a vote gives people a choice as to who they want to represent them in the government
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: factory
body: a factory is a big building full of machines for making things
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That certain jobs are for men only or women only.
body: Just like during the war, anyone should be able to and can do any job.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1964, 51 years after Emily Davison's death, a man called Paul Stephenson walked into the Bay Horse Pub in Bristol.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He ordered a drink, but before he could drink it the manager told him to leave.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Stephenson refused, and eight police officers came to arrest him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He was held in a police cell until midnight.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The manager had told Stephenson to leave because he was black.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pub
body: a place where people can buy drinks is called a pub
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: manager
body: a manager is the person in charge of a place
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: police officer
body: a police officer is a person whose job it is to make sure that people follow the law
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: arrested
body: when someone is arrested, they are taken away by the police because they have broken the law
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that as soon as someone is arrested, they go to prison.
body: This doesn't happen and is not what happened to Paul Stephenson. He was kept in a holding cell in the police station until midnight.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Paul Stephenson was born in 1937 and was evacuated when he was three years old because of the Second World War.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He lived in the countryside for the next seven years and enjoyed paddling in streams and hunting rabbits.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, Paul was always treated differently because he was the only black child.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When he returned to London his classmates made fun of the colour of his skin.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Second World War
body: the Second World War involved lots of countries fighting between 1939 and 1945
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: evacuated
body: when people are evacuated they are moved from a dangerous area to a safer one
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: countryside
body: the countryside means areas with lots of fields which are away from towns and cities
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That evacuation was a negative experience for all children.
body: Lots of children had healthier diets, more freedom and enjoyed their lives in the countryside.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After school Paul joined the RAF and spent time in Germany working with young people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After the RAF he studied youth work and moved to Bristol in 1962.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He was the first black youth worker in Bristol.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At this time many black people had come from the Caribbean to live in Bristol.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Even though they had travelled to Britain to help the country recover after the war, they were not treated well.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: RAF
body: people in the RAF fly planes for Britain’s Royal Air Force to protect the country
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: youth worker
body: a youth worker’s job is to work with and help young people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Caribbean
body: the Caribbean is a group of islands in the Caribbean Sea, which is between North and South America
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that people only came to Britain from the Caribbean.
body: People from all over the world came to Britain, including from places like India and Poland.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One big problem that black people faced in Bristol was finding good jobs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Even though there were not enough workers on the city's buses, people of colour were not allowed to work on them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This made Paul Stephenson very angry and so with four men from the Caribbean islands he decided to take action.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They organised a boycott of the city's buses, supported by students, celebrities and politicians.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After several months, the bus company agreed to allow people of colour to work on the buses.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: protest
body: a public demonstration or action expressing disapproval or objection to a policy, decision, or situation, often aimed at raising awareness or demanding change
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: boycott
body: a situation in which people refuse to buy, use or do something because they do not approve of it
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: politician
body: a politician is a person who works in the government
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that the only people not allowed to work for the Bristol bus companies in 1963 were black people.
body: The bus companies did not allow anyone who was not white to work for them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the month after the boycott, Raghbir Singh became Bristol's first bus conductor who was a person of colour.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, Paul Stephenson continued to fight against the way people of colour were being treated.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This is why he went into The Bay Horse pub; he wanted to make people realise that the boycott was not enough.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The boycott and Paul Stephenson's other work influenced the government to make a change.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1965 and 1968, new laws were passed that said people of colour could not be treated unfairly.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bus conductor
body: a person who works on a bus collecting tickets is called a bus conductor
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: laws
body: laws are a set of rules that everyone has to follow
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: government
body: a government is a group of leaders who make laws and decisions for a country
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that only Paul Stephenson's actions directly led to the 1965 law.
body: Paul's actions had an impact as did many other people's in the 1960s.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Despite living some time apart, both Emily and Paul's stories are similar.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were both angry about something that affected them and other people in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They both fought for equality.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were both prepared to go to prison for what they believed and to try and get things changed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They are both recognised today as brave people who helped to change Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: the Suffragettes were a group of people who wanted women to have the right to vote in Britain
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: when someone is arrested, they are taken away by the police because they have broken the law
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: the right of everyone to receive the same treatment
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for the same thing.
body: Emily Davison and Paul Stephenson were fighting for different change to happen in Britain at different times, around 50 years apart.

body: The idea that people travel and have travelled to other places.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some similarities and differences between things in the past and now.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some similarities and differences between the natural world around them and contrasting environments.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Explorers often travel to places that are unknown to them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Humans have always moved around and explored new places.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Humans explored to find new places to live, new survival essentials, or to escape danger.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that explorers always use a map.
body: Early explorers did not have maps. They often used natural features to navigate by such as rivers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of the earliest seaborne explorers were a group of people known as Polynesians.

body: A long time ago Polynesians spread across the Pacific Ocean using canoes that they built.

body: These canoes had to have a strong hull and sail to travel across the ocean.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Polynesians navigated to new islands by watching the waves and the paths of sea creatures.

body: While the Polynesians were exploring the Pacific Ocean, other humans were exploring the Mediterranean.

body: The ancient Minoans, Phoenecians and Greeks used galleys to transport people and goods around the Mediterranean.

body: Galleys had sails and many oars.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Galleys were also used for warfare and would sometimes ram into each other.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that the Mediterranean is a single country.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Vikings used fast, narrow boats called longboats for trading and raiding.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Longboats had oars, sails, and were both strong and flexible, allowing them to withstand strong waves.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Longboats had flat bottoms, allowing them to sail through shallow water and rivers when the tide was high.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Longboats were often used for raiding and the sailors on board would hang their shields over the sides of the boat.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Viking boats were light and fast, they could even be carried short distances over land to other rivers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Vikings
body: the Vikings were raiders from Scandinavia who attacked and settled in Britain at the time of Aethelflaed and Alfred
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: longboat
body: a longboat was a strong, narrow boat used by the Vikings
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: shield
body: a shield is a large piece of wood or metal with a handle at the back that is used for protection and defence
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: raid
body: a surprise attack
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may have the impression that all Vikings were fierce, scary warriors.
body: Some Vikings were warriors, but not all. Vikings were also traders, farmers and settlers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Vikings used the sun, moon and stars to navigate, and also followed the path of birds and other animals.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some archaeologists have found wooden 'sun-shadow' boards that might have been used by the Vikings to navigate.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Vikings used these techniques to travel long distances.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Vikings sailed far down the rivers of Europe to trading ports and met with traders from the Middle East and Asia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They even travelled as far as Iceland, Greenland and North America.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that archaeologists only dig up bones, like dinosaurs or extinct creatures.
body: Archaeologists work with all sorts of objects from the past, many of the items in museums have been dug up by an archaeologist.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Zheng He was a Chinese admiral and explorer and made his final voyage of discovery in 1432, which would be his furthest.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: First stopping at Changle on the Chinese coast, he ordered the inscription of granite stele describing his journeys.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Zheng He had made six other voyages in the seas of South East Asia and across the Indian Ocean.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These voyages, made in huge 'treasure ships', were to show off Chinese power and force foreign rulers to pay tribute.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Having travelled to East Africa, the expedition returned, but without Zheng He, who had died and was buried at sea.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: China
body: modern day China is a large country in East Asia
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: admiral
body: an admiral is a person in charge of many ships and sailors
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a seafarer is a person who often travels by sea
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: stele
body: a stele is a large piece of carved rock showing a story or information
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that Zheng He went on his voyages by himself.
body: He was admiral of the Chinese fleet. He took many ships and lots of sailors on the voyages.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Zheng He and other Chinese sailors were able to navigate across large distances because of various things they used.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Chinese used strong ships called junks with many large sails.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These ships had a rudder, which allowed the Chinese to steer them without oars, which was easier.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Chinese were the first seafarers to use a compass, which made navigation more simple and reliable.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: junk
body: a Chinese ship with sails and a rudder was called a junk
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: rudder

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: to navigate is to find your way and direct a route either physically or metaphorically
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: compass
body: a tool or device used to show direction, helping you find North, South, East West and the bearings in between
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Chinese ships must have had engines.
body: Engines had not been invented yet. Chinese sailing ships relied on the wind and power of the sea to make long journeys.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Shortly after Zheng He's voyages, an Italian navigator and explorer called John Cabot was living in Bristol.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He was sent by the English king, Henry VII, to find a shorter route to Asia, and to claim new lands for England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He tried to sail across the Atlantic but bad weather, food shortages and arguments with his crew meant he failed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He tried again the next year with a small ship, 'The Matthew', and a crew of just 18, reaching what is now Canada.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The next year, the king sent Cabot on another trip to try and reach even further; Cabot and his ships never returned.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Atlantic Ocean
body: the Atlantic Ocean is the ocean between Europe and the Americas
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Americas
body: the Americas are the continents of North and South America
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Asia

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils might find it confusing that John Cabot sounds like a very English name yet he was Italian.
body: John Cabot is the English version of the name he was born as, Giovanni Caboto. He lived in England for so long he was known by John Cabot.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: European sailors, like John Cabot, had begun to use boats more similar to those of Zheng He.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The boats were pointed at the front and square at the back, with a rudder to help them steer.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The boats had many sails and used rigging to support and control the sails to help them catch as much wind as possible.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: European sailors had also begun to use the compass to navigate, like the Chinese before them, and the astrolabe.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: European sailors, like John Cabot, used lead lines to work out how deep the water they were sailing in was.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: rigging
body: a ship's sails are held up and controlled by ropes known as rigging
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: astrolabe
body: sailors used a tool called an astrolabe to work out how far north or south they were
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: lead line
body: a lead line is a length of rope with a piece of lead attached to it
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think because European seafarers were using the navigation tools, they invented them too.
body: European seafarers didn't invent the astrolabe or compass. Many ancient people navigated by the stars like the Polynesians and Vikings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: John Franklin was a British explorer and an admiral in the Navy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Franklin wanted to find the Northwest Passage, something that no one else had managed to do.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Franklin's ships, the 'Erebus' & the 'Terror', were last seen waiting for ice to clear; none of the 129 crew survived.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1859, a note was found that revealed the ships had been abandoned, stuck in ice, and that Franklin was dead.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: navy
body: the navy is the branch of the armed forces which operates at sea
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pacific Ocean
body: the Pacific Ocean is the ocean between the Americas and Asia
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Northwest Passage
body: the Northwest Passage is a northern sea route between the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that the oceans are totally distinct, separate bodies of water.
body: Large bodies of water like oceans and seas are connected by smaller bodies of water like rivers. You can sail from one ocean to another.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By the time of John Franklin, navigation by sea had become more advanced.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Seafarers used new inventions like sextants and chronometers to work out where they were.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Larger, stronger ships meant that longer voyages were undertaken by European explorers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Franklin's expedition used a new type of ship, steamships, fitted with propellers and a heating system.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During their voyage, Franklin's sailors had to endure freezing temperatures.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: steamship

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: propeller
body: a propeller is something that spins in the water to move a ship forward
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a sextant is a measuring tool that measures the distance between two points
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a chronometer is like a watch, it measures the passage of time
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Inside places (like inside boats) are warmer than outside places.
body: Inside places have shelter from rain, so they're drier, but not necessarily warmer. If a place is cold, everywhere is cold unless heated.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 150 years ago, steam power was replacing sail power for ships.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Wooden-hulled ships, which had been used for thousands of years, were being replaced by iron-hulled ones.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: JMW Turner's painting, The Fighting Temeraire, is symbolic of this process, showing the final journey of the Temeraire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Temeraire, an old ship used in important battles, is being towed by a steam boat on its way to be broken up.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is unlikely that Turner witnessed this event, but he has imagined it to make the point that seafaring was changing.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: steam power
body: something uses steam power when it uses a steam engine to heat water to create steam and movement
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Witness
body: A witness is someone who seems an event, typically a crime take place.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that the ship was called 'The Fighting Temeraire'.
body: 'The Fighting Temeraire' was the name of Turner's painting, the ship was called HMS Temeraire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Just under 200 years ago, a race was underway to see which would be the first steamship to cross the Atlantic.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A British engineer called Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the SS Great Western to try and achieve this.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It was a wooden hulled steamship with masts, sails and a paddle wheel.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SS Great Western was narrowly beaten by the SS Sirius, which became the first steamship to cross the Atlantic.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Brunel then designed and built the SS Great Britain, the first iron steamship with a propeller to cross the Atlantic.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that the 'race across the Atlantic' was an actual race, like on school sports day.
body: At around the same time, people in different places were trying to achieve the same thing, so whoever achieved it first won the 'race'.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SS Great Britain was an iron-hulled steamship and was the world's largest ship at the time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Her role was to carry passengers across the Atlantic, and then to carry passengers to Australia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The passengers were divided into first-class and steerage; first-class paid more and had more luxurious cabins.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Fresh food was taken but would be eaten at the start of the journey.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: First-class passengers had four meals with a huge choice; steerage passengers had to make do with simpler food.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: iron-hulled
body: an iron-hulled boat has its hull made of iron, rather than wood or some other material
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: steerage
body: steerage tickets were the cheapest tickets on the ship and did not include a cabin to sleep in
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that in the past ships only carried sailors, captains or other people working on the ship.
body: About 200 years ago, people began to travel through choice. People that travel on ships but do not work on them are called passengers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William Adams was an English sailor who went on many long voyages about 200 years after Zheng He.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adams wanted to follow in the footsteps of other explorers and travel to Asia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adams sailed across the Atlantic to the Americas with five ships, before crossing the Pacific with only two.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: On the voyage a huge storm sunk one of Adam's boats and he arrived in Japan with just one boat and a very sickly crew.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Adam's voyage took over two years and he chose to stay in Japan, working with a local leader to build ships.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Al-Razi was a doctor who used careful observation to understand why people became sick.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He tested medicines to find better treatments.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He chose a hospital location by observing how slowly meat rotted in clean, healthy air.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He treated rich and poor people alike, listening and learning from each patient he helped.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He shared ideas, and his books spread worldwide, helping doctors for hundreds of years.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils might think that people in the past always believed sickness came from bad spirits or punishment.
body: Remind them that, despite not having our modern scientific understanding of illness and medicine, people in the past knew a great deal about sickness and helping ill people, and worked carefully to discover as much as they could.

body: Copernicus studied the night sky carefully and noticed the planets did not move as people expected them to.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most people believed Earth was at the centre, but Copernicus bravely imagined the Sun at the centre instead.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: His new idea explained why planets moved in loops in the night sky and helped people understand the sky in a new way.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many leaders were shocked by his discovery because it challenged old beliefs they thought were correct.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Later scientists used new tools to test his ideas and proved he was right about Earth moving around the Sun.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A planet is a very large sphere of rock or gas that orbits a star.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: telescope

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The graves of Anglo-Saxon women have provided various objects that provide clues about their lives and status.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One Anglo-Saxon woman's grave in Canterbury seems to be of a high status woman as it contained lots of fine jewellery.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A brooch of foreign silver and garnet, likely to be a gift from the Kentish king, shows women could hold high status.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Girdle-hangers have been found, imitating keys or latch-lifters, suggesting women controlled access to the home.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alongside domestic goods in female graves, they seem to symbolise the idea that women controlled access to the home.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All the coins found at Sutton Hoo were Frankish, showing how well connected Kent and East Anglia were to Europe.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Roman influence continued: Offa made coins making him look like an Emperor with Romulus, Remus and a wolf on the back!
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Whilst major towns collapsed after the Romans left, evidence of coins suggested they grew again under the Anglo-Saxons.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Anglo-Saxon kings such as Offa began to mint their own coins at growing towns in places like London and Canterbury.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These, along with lots of pottery, show how towns grew due to the increasing wealth and trade in Anglo-Saxon Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may believe that Offa was the only Anglo-Saxon king to mint coins.
body: Offa was the first, but other kings minted coins with their head on too. The Archbishop of Canterbury has also been found on coins as well as Offa's queen: Cynethryth.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One of the types of written sources we have from the Anglo-Saxon period are law codes.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The laws concern compensation for injuries people caused each other, suggesting Anglo-Saxon society could be violent.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Compensation differed according to status; the laws set out a strict hierarchy with enslaved people at the bottom.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Unlike men women couldn’t receive compensation but they could own property as some laws mention inheritance for widows.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By looking at who is mentioned and how the law affected them, historians have inferred a lot about Anglo-Saxon society.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For almost 125 years roughly 5,000 bronze artifacts have been exhibited in museums across the world.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were produced in the historic West African Kingdom of Benin which was located in what is now Nigeria.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the British Museum in London there are hundreds of these objects.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 2021 the British Museum received a request from Nigeria to return the bronzes.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Benin bronzes were produced in a place called Benin City, which was the heart of the Benin Kingdom.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Edo people built this city on a plain, which was known for the high mud walls and great ditches that enclosed it.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Beyond the city walls roughly 500 separate villages were separated by further walls making up the suburbs of the city.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The city was well planned with straight roads and square houses and there were even metal palm oil burning street lamps.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Merchants and artisans worked and lived in the city, while farmers lived and worked in the surrounding rainforests.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Benin City was a primitive or undeveloped society.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Kingdom of Benin began in the 1000s CE and reached its peak in the 1400s CE under the rule of Oba Ewuare.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Obas were the rulers of Benin, and the people of Benin believed that they were divine and showed them great respect.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Anyone approaching the Oba did so on their knees and were not allowed to look at him without permission.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Oba lived in a palace where they would meet with their officials and lead religious ceremonies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The British Museum holds many brass wall plaques showing Obas with their attendants conducting these rituals.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Oba

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All Obas of Benin were male.
body: While historically most Obas were, indeed, male, there were exceptions, and a few female rulers, known as "Queen Mothers," held significant influence and power. The Queen Mothers often acted as regents for young kings or played advisory roles.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of the objects held by the British Museum can tell us about the Edo's religious beliefs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One brass statue is a head, decorated with animals, that was used during worship of the god Osun.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Osun was the Edo god of medicine and magic and was believed to command the animals of the rainforest.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The head represents how the Oba was believed to have magic powers like the gods; the birds represent prophesy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The snakes represent Osun's soldiers and the Oba's ability to use magic to destroy his enemies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Oba in Edo society was merely a religious figure.
body: While the Oba did have significant religious functions and was seen as having a special connection to the divine, his role also extended to that of political leader, responsible for governance, justice, and maintaining order within the kingdom.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the 1500s CE Portugese merchants began to trade goods like guns with Benin in exchange for enslaved people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Dutch, French and English entered this trade in the 1600s CE, making Benin rich and powerful.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, by the 1800s CE, the power of Benin had weakened, and the British wanted to control trade in the region.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1897 they invaded the kingdom of Benin, burning Benin City to the ground and making it part of British Nigeria.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During the invasion thousands of pieces of Edo artwork, including some of those in the British Museum, were looted.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Kingdom of Benin's trade with Europe solely revolved around the transatlantic slave trade.
body: While the Kingdom of Benin did participate in the slave trade to some extent, it also engaged in other forms of trade, including the exchange of goods such as ivory, pepper, cloth, and brassware.

body: Whether or not the British Museum should return its Benin Bronzes has caused lots of arguments.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the USA, descendants of West African enslaved people are trying to stop the return of Edo artwork to Nigeria.

body: In 1993 archaelogists discovered a magnificent tomb in the Honduran city complex of Copán.

body: The Maya lived in a part of central America called Mesoamerica.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Mesoamerica contained rich fertile lands in the highlands and plains, and humid rainforests in the lowlands.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: From about 750 BCE, the Maya built cities like Copán near rivers, just like other early civilisations.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These were all different, but usually contained a ceremonial centre with temple-pyramids, ballcourts and palaces.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They often contained causeways and standing stones carved with pictures and writings about their rulers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Mesoamerica
body: Mesoamerica is an area of land that stretches from the southern part of North America and extends to the Pacific coast of Central America
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Mesoamerican civilizations were primitive or less advanced compared to European counterparts.
body: Mesoamerican societies achieved remarkable advancements in architecture, mathematics, astronomy, agriculture, and writing systems. E.g., the Maya developed calendar systems and made contributions to mathematics, including the concept of zero.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In another Maya city, Yaxchilán, a carved stone lintel has helped archaeologists to understand a lot about Maya beliefs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It shows a bloodletting ritual performed by Yaxchilán's king, Shield Jaguar the Great, and his wife, Lady K’ab’al Xook.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Lady K’ab'al Xook pulled a thorned rope through her tongue to make it bleed so that she could speak with the gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bloodletting was important to the Maya; they believed the gods had let their blood to create the human race.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By bloodletting, Maya rulers showed their thanks to the gods, but also showed that they were the right people to rule.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: lintel
body: a lintel is the beam such as a piece of stone or wood over a door or window which supports the bricks above the door or window
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bloodletting
body: bloodletting was the practice of cutting part of the body to release blood
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Bloodletting was a common and widespread practice among all Maya individuals on a regular basis.
body: Bloodletting rituals were primarily performed by the Maya elite, such as rulers, priests, and nobles, and were often reserved for specific ceremonial occasions or important events.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya believed the sky was where the gods lived; watching it carefully they tracked the movement of celestial bodies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya had lots of different calendars, some were based on these movements, others on the time it took maize to grow.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya used these calendars to make sure they carried out religious ceremonies at the right times and to measure time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya used cycles to measure time, so their calendars were circular and relied on great mathematical understanding.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Using these calendars, the Maya recorded the dates of when important things happened, using their hieroglyphic writing.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: calendar

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Maya had just one calendar.
body: They actually used several interconnected calendars. The most notable ones are the Tzolk'in (a 260-day ceremonial calendar), the Haab' (a 365-day solar calendar), and the Long Count calendar, which tracked longer periods of time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the tombs of Maya rulers, archaeologists have found decorated pots that once contained a special drink.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This hot chocolate drink was made from roasting and boiling the fruit of a plant called cacao.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya took care preparing hot chocolate, frothing it carefully, because they believed it was a gift from the gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Another crop that the Maya thought was sacred was maize; it was used to make flat pancakes called tortillas.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya believed that the gods tried for a long time to make humans, and only succeeded when they used maize to do so.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cacao

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: maize

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Cacao is the same as cocoa.
body: While they come from the same source, the cacao bean, there are differences in processing. Cacao generally refers to the raw or minimally processed form of the bean, while cocoa usually refers to the processed and roasted form.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Maya have a lot in common with other early civilisations from around the world.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, they were also distinctive compared with other early civilisations e.g. they were a stone age society.

body: The Maya's advanced understanding of maths and astronomy and bloodletting was very important in their religion.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Maya were a single, unified empire.
body: They were organised into independent city-states with their own rulers, languages, and alliances. While they shared cultural traits and religious beliefs, they were politically fragmented entities that sometimes engaged in conflicts with each other.
