body: After Alfred’s treaty with Guthrum, he controlled much of Mercia but made himself their overlord instead of their king.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alfred married his daughter, Aethelflaed to Mercia’s most powerful man: Aethelred.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Aethelflaed was heavily involved in rebuilding Mercia following Viking occupation by building burhs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Her rule was strengthened by her piety; she built a priory at Gloucester which housed the recaptured bones of St Oswald.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 902, her older husband was sick and Aethelflaed defeated Vikings at Chester in 907.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: overlord

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may not realise the significant leading role Aethelflaed had during this time.
body: Aethelflaed was thought to have been a strong, independent and well-educated woman. She had learnt a great deal about military leadership and strategy by watching her father King Alfred.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After her husband’s death in 911, Aethelflaed worked with her brother Edward, King of Wessex to attack the Vikings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She captured Tamworth, Mercia’s old capital, and used it as a base from which to drive back the Vikings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the same time, her brother Edward won numerous victories against the Vikings in East Anglia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 917 Aethelflaed launched an assault on the Viking town of Derby, capturing it, followed by Leicester soon after.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: On the eve of Aethelflaed's death in 918, only York remained as a Viking stronghold.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: formidable
body: when something is formidable it inspires fear or respect through being impressively large, powerful, or capable
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may not understand that it was a combination of factors that led to laying the foundations of England.
body: Aethelflaed and Edward were able to lay the foundations for England by establishing strongholds to protect their towns and cities, combining their forces and leading campaigns together.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Despite fighting the Vikings and uniting the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, Aetheflaed's story has often been forgotten.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One possible reason for this is because her brother Edward wanted to make sure that Mercia stayed loyal to him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Edward wanted Mercia to submit to him, and not stay loyal to his sister's memory.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is likely that Edward made sure that the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle mentioned a lot about him instead of Aethelflaed.

body: Michael Wood is one historian who has tried to tell Aethelflaed's story because it is the story of England's beginning.

body: Female leaders, like Aethelflaed, are often written out of history as there was prejudice towards women. Despite Aethelflaed's success and the respect she gained, she was likely erased from history so it did not undermine male leaders at the time.

body: In 925, Edward’s son, Athelstan, was consecrated King of Mercia and Wessex with a crown: a new ceremony of coronation.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 927, Athelstan captured the last Viking stronghold, York and began to mint coins bearing the title ‘rex Anglorum’.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The north had not had a southern king; Athelstan assembled the rulers of Scotland and Northumbria to submit to him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Welsh kings already recognised the overlordship of the King of Wessex.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Athelstan was now the overlord of all of Britain and some historians have called him the first ‘King of England’.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Athelstan’s reign did not see the end of the Vikings in England, with continued raids and uprisings in Northumbria.

body: In 1013, Sweyn Forkbeard captured the whole of England before dying.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Canute became King of England, Norway and Denmark, creating a huge North Sea empire which English trade benefited from.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: His son Harthacnut succeeded him in 1035 and ruled for seven years until an Anglo-Saxon, Edward, took the throne.

body: World War One had many fronts; battles were fought on the Western Front, the Eastern Front, in Africa and in Asia.

body: He fought at one of the most famous battles of WWI: the Battle of the Somme.

body: While men were sent to the front, the war also had an impact on those who stayed behind.

body: Like the Ancient Romans, whose beliefs had been influenced by the Ancient Greeks, the Celtic people were polytheistic.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In Britain, the Ancient Romans introduced their own gods and wiped out the druids (Celtic religious leaders) in 60CE.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Elsewhere the Ancient Romans were tolerant of Celtic religion, allowing it to continue alongside some of their gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Evidence shows us that religious change was slow, and often in combination with existing beliefs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polytheism
body: when people believe in many gods and goddesses, it is called polytheism
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: barbarian
body: a barbarian was what the Ancient Romans called anyone who did not follow Greek or Roman traditions
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: druids
body: the druids were priests of the Celtic religion who believed they could communicate with their gods and goddesses
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ancestor
body: an ancestor is someone's family member from the past

title: Pupils may gain the impression that the Ancient Romans destroyed all aspects of Celtic worship.
body: Remind pupils that although the druids were wiped out, the worship of Celtic gods was tolerated as long as Ancient Roman ones were also respected.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Celtic buildings were usually thatched, wattle and daub roundhouses.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists can look at the remains of buildings to construct arguments about the impact of the Romans in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Evidence of North African Roman soldiers has been found at Hadrian’s Wall, a major Ancient Roman architectural feature.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Caerwent, Trimontium and Bath are all places that have examples of the sorts of architecture the Ancient Romans built.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rich Ancient Romans built villas in the British countryside with expensive mosaics and hypocaust systems for heating.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: thatched
body: thatched roofs were made from a type of plant material, like straw
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wattle and daub
body: buildings made up of woven twigs and rods that have been covered in clay are called wattle and daub
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Hadrian’s Wall
body: Hadrian's Wall was a long wall the Romans built in the north of England to defend it from Celtic tribes
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hypocaust system
body: a hypocaust system was an Ancient Roman underfloor heating system
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that Hadrian's Wall was not very high, as the remaining stretches have been damaged.
body: Remind pupils that Hadrian's Wall is over a thousand years old, and any sections still standing were much taller in the past.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The largest settlements built by the Celts were small hillforts.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Romans introduced towns, connected by roads across Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cirencester (Corinium Dobunnorum) was Roman Britain's second largest town.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Towns like Cirencester were designed in grids with the forum in the centre and some had aqueducts.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some big towns like Cirencester had amphitheatres which were used for public entertainment.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hillfort
body: a Celtic hillfort was built on top of a hill and surrounded by wooden fences for protection
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: amphitheatre
body: an amphitheatre was a large arena that hosted public entertainment like gladiator fights
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: forum
body: a forum was an important area in the middle of an Ancient Roman town where people would meet
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: aqueduct
body: an aqueduct was a series of bridges used to transport clean drinking water to towns
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that all people in Roman Britain lived in Roman towns.
body: Make it clear to pupils that although many people came to the towns, Britain remained largely rural, with lots of small Celtic settlements.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many Celtic people adopted Ancient Roman ways of life, but some resisted.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ancient Roman religions were adopted in Britain but often overlapped with older beliefs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ancient Roman town building created major urban centres for the first time, connected by paved roads.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Roman settlement meant that people and goods from many countries travelled to Britain e.g. the Ivory Bangle Lady.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many aspects of life changed for people in Britain, and resistance to Ancient Roman rule and culture varied.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romano-British
body: Romano-British culture is a mix of Roman and old British ways of living
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Ivory Bangle Lady
body: the Ivory Bangle Lady was an Ancient Roman with North African family whose skeleton was found in York
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that all aspects of religion, or all aspects of buildings changed.
body: Remind pupils that within an area of study that we define, there can be elements of both change and continuity.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The changes that had taken place in Britain during the Stone and Bronze Ages.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The changes that had taken place in Britain during the Iron Age.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An awareness of artifacts and how archaeologists interact with them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An awareness of ancient civilisations and peoples as producers of art.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1984, workers at a peat bog in North West England made an incredible discovery: the preserved body of a man.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists aren't sure exactly when he died, but it was some time around the end of the Iron Age in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By looking at this preserved body, archaeologists have been able to work out all sorts of things about Iron Age Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, there are many questions that they still have about him and the time and society in which he lived.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: peat
body: peat is a type of soil formed in bogs over a long period of time
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: archaeologist
body: an archaeologist is someone who studies human history by looking at artefacts
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bog
body: a bog is an area of wet, muddy ground
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: preserved
body: when something is preserved it is protected from damage or loss
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That all bodies remain in a preserved state after death.
body: Explain that after death the body normally decomposes and a skeleton remains.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Iron Age Britain was dominated by a group of people called the Celts, who had spread across Europe.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Art was very important to the Celts, who made large numbers of metal objects in a style known as La Tène.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Snettisham Great Torc shows the incredible artistry and craftsmanship the Celts were capable of.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Battersea Shield made of bronze shows incredible craftmanship and the distinctive swirling patterns of La Tène.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists have worked out that it was too thin for protection, and so was probably an offering to the gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Celts
body: Celts were groups of people living in Britain and across Europe during the Iron Age
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: La Tène
body: a popular later style of Celtic art which uses curves, swirls and leafy patterns is called La Tène
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: torc
body: a torc is a large solid ring worn around the neck
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that all of our knowledge of the Iron Age is definitely correct.
body: Explain that archaeologists use artefacts to learn about the past, they get ideas and clues from the artefacts and build up a picture of what they think the past was like. There is very little written evidence about the Celts.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 2001 in northern England, a grave was discovered of someone who must have been very important.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Inside the grave, alongside the bones, were the remains of an Iron Age chariot.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All that remained of the chariot were its metal parts and highly decorated bronze fittings, some inlaid with coral.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The grave therefore suggests that chariots were important in Celtic warfare in Britain during the Iron Age.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When the Romans came to Britain for the first time in the 1st century BCE, they noted that the Celts used chariots.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chariot
body: a chariot is a wheeled vehicle pulled by horses, often used in war
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: coral
body: the hard skeleton of a type of tiny sea animal is called coral
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romans
body: the Romans were a group of people from Italy that took over lots of land across Europe, Africa and the Middle East
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That the archaeologists used the actual artefacts found in the grave to make the reconstruction of the chariot.
body: Ensure pupils understand that archaeologists used new materials to make a replica chariot based on the evidence in the grave.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The bones of the person buried with the Wetwang chariot have led archaeologists to think she was a woman.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The care taken to bury her, her chariot and other goods (a mirror and a brooch) suggest she was very important.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This has led them to believe that women could be powerful warriors and rulers in the Iron Age, just like men.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Later on, Ancient Roman writers also noted this, describing how women fought alongside men.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historians think that Celtic women could become rulers in their own right and own and inherit their own land.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: warrior
body: a brave or experienced soldier or fighter
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tribe
body: a tribe is a group of people, families, or villages that share the same language, customs, and ancestors
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inherit
body: to receive money, property or possessions from someone after the person has died
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some may think that Celtic people and Iron Age people lived in different time periods.
body: Celtic people lived during the Iron Age.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By examining the bones of the warrior woman buried with the Wetwang chariot archaeologists think she came from Gaul.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This has led them to understand that Celtic Britain had connections to mainland Europe during the Iron Age.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists have found other evidence to support this, such as golden coins that were minted in France and Belgium.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Evidence from the east of England shows that a leader called Cunobelin imported luxury goods from the Roman Empire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cunobelin even minted his own coins in the style of Roman ones, showing that these were familiar to Celtic Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Gaul
body: Gaul was an ancient region of Western Europe which included France, Belgium, Luxembourg, and parts of Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany, and Northern Italy
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: luxury goods
body: objects that are expensive and not a necessity are described as luxury goods
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: minted
body: when coins are made they are said to be minted
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That by connected we mean geographically or physically rather thank via communication and trade.
body: Discuss the meaning of the word connected. Explore maps of the areas concerned. Explain that Britain and Europe were connected by communication and trade.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists and historians have learnt a lot about Iron Age Britain from the artefacts that have been found.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They have used these artefacts alongside other sources, such as Roman writing about Iron Age Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By using these sources together they have been able to piece together what Iron Age Britain was like.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historians and archaeologists rarely rely on just one source, they often try to use lots together.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A good explanation of what historians have learnt about Iron Age Britain will focus on how sources have been used.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: someone or something that supplies information
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That archaeologists and historians are always right. That information about the past is always factual.
body: Explain that archaeologists and historians use clues to piece together what they think the past was like. These views and opinions can change over time as more sources or information is discovered.

body: The Second World War broke out in 1939 when Nazi Germany invaded Poland.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Having promised to defend Poland, Britain and France declared war on Nazi Germany.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When war was declared, many men and women joined the armed forces.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The war lasted six years and brought about significant changes for many people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Second World War has been seen as a turning point because the changes it brought were decisive and permanent.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Nazi Germany
body: When Germany was governed by a group of people called the Nazis it was called Nazi Germany.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Poland
body: Poland is a country that lies between Germany and Russia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ration
body: When there is not enough of something, a ration is the small amount that each person is allowed to have equally.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Only British people fought for Britain during the Second World War.
body: Highlight how millions of men and women from around the world helped the British armed forces.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Before the Second World War, women were expected to take care of domestic matters rather than working.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If women did work, they were mainly employed in shops, domestic service or nursing - jobs thought to be ‘women’s jobs’.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In December 1941, women were conscripted for the first time in British history; they could now do ‘men’s jobs’.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Women worked in munitions, aircraft and tank factories, in shipbuilding or farming.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Women also joined the armed forces as part of the WAAF, ATS or WRNS.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: domestic
body: relating to inside a home or to family relations, this can also refer to existing or occurring inside a particular country; not foreign or international
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: domestic service
body: working in someone else's home is known as domestic service
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conscription
body: the act or process of forcing people by law to join the armed services
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that only women from Britain served in the armed forces.
body: Highlight how thousands of women from across the British Empire at the time joined organisations like the ATS to help the British war effort.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Second World War was fought across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During the war, soldiers from all over the British Empire and Commonwealth fought against Nazi Germany and their allies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Before the war, most people in Britain would only rarely travel abroad or meet people from other countries.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With large numbers of British soldiers mixing with Empire and Commonwealth troops this changed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In Britain itself, many people travelled from across the Empire to assist the war effort, bringing ethnic diversity.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: empire
body: an empire is a group of countries or provinces ruled from the centre by a person or group of people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Allied Forces
body: the Allied Forces included Britain and those countries that fought with Britain in WWII
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ethnic diversity
body: ethnic diversity refers to many people from different ethnic and cultural backgrounds
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some pupils may think that the fighting in the Second World War only happened in Europe.
body: Discuss how the fighting was global and happened across three different continents with millions of people worldwide involved.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Second World War saw mass bombing campaigns against British civilians for the first time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Nazi Germany targeted British cities in 1940-1941, hoping to destroy British industry and morale.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The government had prepared for this by evacuating many children away from the cities the moment the war started.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For many city children, this was the first time they had been to the countryside, seen farm animals or eaten vegetables.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For many children, away from home for so long, returning to their old lives and families in the city was very difficult.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: civilian
body: a civilian is someone who is not part of the armed forces
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bombing
body: dropping explosives out of an aeroplane onto the ground below is called bombing
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: evacuee
body: a person who has been moved to another place for safety is an evacuee
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: morale
body: morale is a feeling of positivity about what is happening
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that children were only evacuated to areas in Britain during the Second World War.
body: Children were sent to other countries like Australia and South Africa in 1940.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Nursing in the Second World War brought new people to Britain and helped new medical techniques to succeed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead new plastic surgery techniques were trialled on badly injured soldiers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sister Mary Meally ran the burns ward, where she looked after badly burnt airmen who were receiving treatment.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many West African and Caribbean women travelled to, and trained as nurses in Britain during World War II.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These included Princess Ademola, daughter of the Alake of Abeokuta, an important king in Nigeria.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: plastic surgery
body: surgery that involves the reconstruction or repair of the body is called plastic surgery
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Nigeria
body: Nigeria is a large West African country situated on the Atlantic Ocean
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that nurses only did tasks like cleaning wards and providing meals.
body: Nurses did three years of training and had to pass exams in anatomy and physiology. They handled weapons on the front line and ran the hospitals caring for the injured in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During the Second World War the experiences of men, women and children differed greatly.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: However, the great changes that the Second World War brought about affected a large number of people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Because of the global nature of the war British people were exposed to unfamiliar places, cultures and ways of life.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Second World War was a turning point for many women and for children because it changed their lives forever.

body: Early Christianity spread from Judea throughout the Roman Empire, reaching Roman Britain in the late 2nd century CE.

body: At first Christians were persecuted in the Roman Empire as their faith worried the Romans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Christians were scapegoated and punished severely, often by being attacked and killed by wild animals in amphitheatres.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many Christians were killed for their faith, making them martyrs.

body: By 312 CE, Constantine had become the emperor of the Western Roman Empire by defeating his rivals in many battles.

body: Constantine converted to Christianity, saying all religions could be practised and Christians should not be persecuted.

body: In 324 CE, Constantine became sole emperor of the Roman Empire and in 330 CE created a new eastern capital.

body: In 325 CE, Constantine brought together Christian bishops to try to agree the first set of rules about Christianity.

title: The Byzantines weren’t Roman.
body: The Byzantine Empire, also known as the Eastern Roman Empire, was a continuation of the Roman Empire. The term "Byzantine" is a modern designation used by historians, but the people of that time considered themselves Romans.

body: Christian Churches did not just emerge in the Western Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In Ethiopia today, many Aksumite churches have been found carved into rocky mountainsides.

body: Around 3,000 years before Jesus was born, an ancient civilisation was flourishing between two large rivers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It was called Sumer, and it sat between the Tigris and the Euphrates rivers in a place called Mesopotamia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These rivers made it an ideal place to grow crops due to the soil being fertile, just like the Nile in Egypt.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Sumerians did not just rely on the flooding of the rivers to make farming better.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They built ditches and channels to divert water from the rivers to their fields, creating a reliable water supply.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: civilisation
body: a civilisation is a well organised group of people that has their own language and way of life
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Sumer
body: Sumer was the earliest ancient civilisation to be known about and was located in the south of Mesopotamia
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Mesopotamia
body: meaning 'between two rivers', Mesopotamia is the name given to the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: reliable is another word for trustworthy and accurate
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think floods are only destructive.
body: Explain that floodwaters can be very dangerous and cause much damage, but they also bring water and nutrients to the land for growing crops.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Mesopotamian civilisations like the Sumerians were able to trade their extra food with people who lived far away.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists think that as these civilisations traded more they needed a way of recording what was being traded.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They began to write down and count what they were giving and receiving in a special writing called cuneiform.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Because their farming was productive, they could stay in one place, and so they built cities with large stone buildings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of the biggest of these stone buildings were called ziggurats, which were large, stepped religious buildings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Mesopotamia and the Nile were not the only places where people stopped moving around and settled down to farm.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In Asia, other civilisations developed in the Indus River Valley and the Yellow River Valley.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historians and archaeologists sometimes use the phrase 'cradles of civilisation' to describe these places.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As in Egypt and Mesopotamia, the people of the Indus and the Yellow River Valleys channeled water for farming.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As in Egypt and Mesopotamia, the people of the Indus and the Yellow River Valleys created cities and art.

title: Egypt and Mesopotamia are the only places to have had early civilisations.
body: Look at a map of the world and point out the locations of the Indus Valley and Shang civilisations.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The early civilisations that developed in the 'cradles of civilisation' all produced art and beautiful objects.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They carved statues out of stone or formed them from clay.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They made pottery and painted or pressed decorative patterns into them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When they discovered how to mix tin and copper to make bronze, this was used to make many pieces of art.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Despite similarities in how they were made these civilisations all had their own styles of art.

title: Art is only drawings or paintings.
body: Look at lots of different examples of ancient art, such as sculpture, textiles, jewellery, decorated household objects, weapons and armour.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Despite having different gods and goddesses, all of these ancient civilisations built special religious buildings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many of them, like the Shang, the Egyptians and the Indus people, offered sacrifices to their gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All of these civilisations produced writing about trade, religion, laws and rulers.

title: Ancient writing was only for stories about rulers and gods.
body: Discuss the four different uses of ancient writing: trade, laws, religion and rulers. Discuss how these are similar to modern use, like laws needed for an ancient civilisation to develop, and think about the kinds of laws they would have needed.

body: All of these early civilisations left a nomadic lifestyle because they found ways of farming fertile ground near rivers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All of them built permanent places to live like cities, along with other buildings for the purpose of religion.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All of these early civilisations traded with people from far away and developed their own forms of writing.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All of these early civilisations made bronze and used this metal for tools, weapons and artwork.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Natural climate change has meant that different groups of humans have come to and left Britain at different times.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Stone tools and footprints at Happisburgh show that the first known Britons came to Britain c. 950,000 years ago.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Around 500,000 years ago teeth and bones found at Boxgrove show Homo heidelbergensis lived in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ice Ages around 450,000 and 20,000 years ago resulted in long periods when no humans lived in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Homo sapiens came to Britain c. 40,000 years ago, left during the most recent Ice Age and returned c. 12,000 years ago.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Paleolithic Era took place between two million years ago and ten thousand years ago.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many of the types of Paleolithic human who lived in Britain used stone tools, which were often made of flint.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These tools, especially hand axes, are some of the main sources of evidence archaeologists have for this period.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists have worked out how Paleolithic humans might have used their hand axes.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists think that they probably used them to skin animals for clothing and strip branches for fire and shelter.

body: The Neolithic Era saw lots of changes for early humans in Britain.

body: Animal bones found during excavations suggest that this is when humans began to domesticate animals such as cattle.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This was the first time that people started deliberately planting and harvesting crops.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Excavations at Skara Brae have unearthed barley seeds, suggesting cultivation.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: New technologies developed: this is the first period from which archaeologists find pottery, including at Skara Brae.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Neolithic Era
body: the Neolithic Era is also known as the New Stone Age and is the third and final part of the Stone Age
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That all Neolithic houses were built from stone.
body: Explain that many Neolithic house in Britain were built from wood and daub. Houses at Skara Brae were built from stone as no wood was available.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists have discovered many different artefacts from across the Stone Age.

body: The types of artefacts found show the changes that have taken place throughout the period.

body: In Mesopotamia, where Sumer had once flourished, warring city-states continued to vie for supremacy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cyrus, king of Persian Achaemenids, conquered the kingdom of Medes and the city of Babylon, creating the Persian Empire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cyrus' son Cambyses went on to conquer Egypt, so that the pharoahs were now controlled by Persia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 490 BCE, a king named Darius ruled over the Persian Empire, adding to it with territory in the Indus Valley.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Darius wanted to add the Greek city-states to his empire and so the two civilisations went to war.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Mesopotamia
body: meaning 'between two rivers', Mesopotamia is the name given to the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Sumer
body: Sumer was the earliest ancient civilisation to be known about and was located in the south of Mesopotamia
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Persian Empire
body: the civilisation that rivalled Ancient Greece to its east was Persia, all the lands they ruled were the Persian Empire
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: territory
body: a territory is an area of land that is far away from a country but is still ruled by the country
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Indus Valley
body: the Indus Valley surrounds the River Indus, a powerful river that flows through India and Pakistan
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That the historical places named still exist today.
body: Over time, names and boundaries of places can change. Some places cease to exist entirely while the locations of some places do still exist but they have a different name today. A large area of Persia for example is in the modern-day country of Iran.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The first major battle between the Greek city-states and Persia was at Marathon.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Persian army fought its way onto the beach before being repulsed; a runner was sent to declare victory in Athens.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The new Persian king Xerxes attacked Greece by land, taking days to defeat a small band of Greeks at Thermopylae.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Persians then captured Athens, destroying the temple atop the acropolis before the sea-battle of Salamis.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At Salamis, the Persians were defeated, preventing Persia from conquering Greece.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conquer
body: to conquer means to take control of another place
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: runner
body: in this lesson, a runner is a messenger who carries messages by running between places
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: acropolis
body: the fortified hill of an ancient Greek city was called an acropolis
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sea-battle
body: when boats are used to attack an enemy during a war, this is a sea-battle
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That battles are always fought on land, by soldiers or warriors who are physically fighting each other.
body: Battles can be fought many ways - some Ancient Greek battles were land based and warriors used chariots and weapons like javelins. Other battles were at sea using boats that would be rammed into the enemy and archers that would fire arrows at them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During the wars between Greece and Persia the north-eastern Greek kingdom of Macedon had ended up under Persian control.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Eventually the Greeks of Macedon pushed the Persians out and Alexander's father, Philip came to rule as King of Macedon.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Philip built Macedon into a powerful kingdom, convincing other city-states to join him, creating the League of Corinth.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Philip created the League of Corinth to defeat Persia once and for all, but he was murdered before he could achieve it.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Philip's son Alexander, tutored by Aristotle from Athens, was now King of Macedon and led Greece against Persia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Macedon
body: Macedon was a kingdom in the north east of Ancient Greece
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: kingdom
body: a kingdom is a country or area ruled by a king or queen
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Persia
body: the civilisation that rivalled Ancient Greece to its east was Persia, sometimes called the Persian Empire
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That the Kingdom of Macedon and the modern republic of North Macedonia are the same place.
body: Although North Macedonia's name stems from Macedon, they are not exactly the same location. Most of North Macedonia was part of Macedon, but Macedon also covered large parts of what is now northern Greece, southern Bulgaria and eastern Albania.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In his first battle against the Persians, Alexander showed great bravery and won the respect of his soldiers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexander captured city after Persian city, showing the people great mercy before defeating Darius III at Issus.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexander then marched into Egypt, where the people made him pharaoh as thanks for ridding them of their Persian rulers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexander then sought out Darius III, defeating him at Gaugamela with superior tactics against the Persian chariots.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexander conquered Babylon before continuing east to the River Indus; he died whilst returning home with his army.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mercy
body: showing mercy is treating someone kindly when you have power over them
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pharaoh
body: the leaders of Ancient Egypt were called pharaohs
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tactics
body: plans you create and use to win or succeed
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Babylon
body: Babylon was an ancient city in the Persian Empire that was located on the Euphrates River
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That only Egyptian people who were related by blood to the previous pharaoh could become a pharaoh.
body: Alexander was an ancient Greek. He was not Egyptian by birth or by blood but the Egyptian people still made him a pharaoh after Alexander drove the Persians out of Egypt.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Defeating the Persian Empire and expanding Greek control into Egypt and India were not Alexander's only achievements.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He sliced the famous Gordian knot in two and conquered Babylon, a city the Greeks could scarcely imagine.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He founded the great city of Alexandria in Egypt, which came to be ruled by one of his generals, Ptolemy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ptolemy and his son tried to turn Alexandria into the greatest of all Greek cities, building an incredible library.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexandria became a centre of learning which attracted brilliant minds like Euclid and Galen.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Alexandria is a city in Greece.
body: Alexander the Great founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt, not on the mainland or any island of Ancient Greece. There is still a city called Alexandria on the original site in Egypt today; some ruins of the ancient city can be visited by tourists.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'The Great' is not a title that Alexander had during his lifetime; it is an epithet, given to him after his death.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Romans, who grew in power some time after Alexander, admired his achievements and used this epithet for him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alexander is remembered as 'Great' due to his military prowess: never losing a battle and personally leading his men.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He has also been named 'The Great' for managing to keep his vast empire united, although it fragmented after his death.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In founding Alexandria, which went on to become a hugely important centre of learning, he has also been seen as 'Great'.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Epithet

title: Ancient Romans
body: the Ancient Romans were a group of people from Italy that took over lots of land across Europe, Africa and the Middle East
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: prowess
body: exceptional skill or ability, especially in a particular field or activity
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Alexander 'The Great' was the title that Alexander had when he was a living ruler.
body: 'The Great' is not a title. It is a type of nickname called an epithet. Epithets are only used to refer to people that have died and they tell us more about something significant the person did or what the person was like.

body: At one time there were two Egyptian kingdoms: Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt, but around 3,000 BCE they were united.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The civilisation known as the Ancient Egyptians began over 3,000 years before the birth of Christ, 3,000 BC or BCE.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They lived near a large river they called the Nile, in North Africa, protected from enemies by dry land to their sides.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The River Nile was long, deep and filled with a dark black mud.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When the Nile flooded, this mud made the land the Egyptians live on turn black, and become very fertile.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: civilisation
body: a civilisation is a well organised group of people that has their own language and way of life
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: BC is short for 'Before Christ' and refers to the time before the year 1, in which people believe Jesus was born
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that the River Nile is a river found only in Egypt.
body: The River Nile does flow through Egypt, but it also flows through 10 other countries in east Africa. It is Africa's longest river.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The ruler of Ancient Egypt was called the pharaoh; they owned all the land, made all the laws and taxed their subjects.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The pharaohs, whose subjects believed to be both gods and humans, ruled in the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: During the Old Kingdom the Ancient Egyptians built pyramids to bury their pharaohs in, the most famous at Giza.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Middle Kingdom Egypt grew rich and strong, stopped using pyramids and buried pharaohs in the Valley of the Kings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the New Kingdom Egypt grew stronger, using their chariots and strong bronze weapons to take over more land.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: laws
body: laws are a set of rules that everyone has to follow
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: taxes
body: everyone has to pay money called taxes to the people in charge of a country
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: subjects
body: subjects are the people controlled by a ruler
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pyramid
body: the pyramids were large stone buildings that the Ancient Egyptians buried their pharaohs in during the Old Kingdom
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chariot
body: a chariot is a wheeled vehicle pulled by horses, often used in war
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that the kingdoms are places in Egypt.
body: Kingdoms are are periods of time in Egyptian history; the Old Kingdom, the Middle Kingdom and the New Kingdom.

body: On the 6 November 1922, an excavation in the Valley of the Kings led by Howard Carter discovered something incredible.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: His team discovered a set of stone steps leading down a doorway covered in hieroglyphs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Inside the doorway Carter could see a room filled with beautiful objects made from precious woods and metals.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Howard Carter and his team had discovered the tomb of an Egyptian ruler called Tutankhamun.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: He was buried with objects as Egyptians believed he needed them in the afterlife and they wanted to show off his wealth.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: excavation
body: an excavation is a project to dig something from the past out of the ground
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Valley of the Kings
body: the Valley of the Kings is a part of Egypt where many pharaohs were buried in tombs
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hieroglyphics
body: the Ancient Egyptians wrote using a kind of writing called hieroglyphics; each symbol and picture was called a hieroglyph
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tomb
body: a tomb is a large stone structure built to bury the dead.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may find it hard to comprehend the slow and painstaking nature of carrying out excavations.
body: Carter began excavating the Valley of the Kings many years before finding Tutankhamun's tomb; they were about to give up when they found it.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In Rosetta, some hundred years before Carter's discovery of Tutankhamun, some soldiers dug up a large black stone.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It was covered in both Greek and hieroglyphic writing; archaeologists used the Greek to translate the hieroglyphs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These hieroglyphs were pictures, rather than words, and there were more than 1,000 of them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Scribes would write in hieroglyphs to record things the pharaohs said or did and to compose religious messages.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Over time scribes wanted to make hieroglyphs simpler and eventually they were only used for religious writings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Rosetta
body: Rosetta is a city in Egypt where the Rosetta Stone was found
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Translate
body: To translate something means to change it from one language to another.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: scribe
body: a scribe is someone who is trained to write or copy things
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: something that concerns religion is described as religious

title: That there was one hieroglyph (picture) equivalent to each letter of the English alphabet.
body: The Ancient Egyptians did not have an alphabet in the same way we do today. Hieroglyphs represented sounds and sometimes whole words. There were a lot more hieroglyphs than there are letters of the alphabet.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Egyptians believed in many gods; one of these was Anubis, who guided the souls of the dead to the afterlife.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Egyptians believed that when they died they would go to the afterlife if they had pleased the gods.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They believed that everybody had a soul, and that when somone was dead, their soul returned to their body each night.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This led them to try and preserve dead bodies with linen and by drying them in sand but with only partial success.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By the end of the Old Kingdom they had started to embalm and mummify the bodies, placing the organs in canopic jars.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: afterlife
body: Ancient Egyptians believed that there was life after death which they called the afterlife
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: soul
body: Ancient Egyptians believed that the soul is a part of a human, that it is separate from the body and that it is the centre of feeling and thought
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ba
body: the Ancient Egyptians used the word ba for someone's soul
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: preserving a dead body through embalming and cloth wrapping is known as mummification
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: the Ancient Egyptians placed a dead person's organs inside canopic jars during the mummification process
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That mummification is just a case of wrapping a body in bandages and burying it.
body: There are several stages in the mummification process, each of which must be done precisely and carefully in order to be successful.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The River Nile remained the heart of the civilisation and was always highly important for the fertility it brought.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The pharaohs ruled throughout this time, but where and how they were buried changed over time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: While beliefs about the afterlife stayed the same, the methods of preserving bodies became very advanced over time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Detailed hieroglyphs were used throughout, but gradually were used less and usually just for religious writings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A good description of how much things stayed the same will use knowledge from throughout this unit.

body: The Trojan War was a mythical conflict between the Ancient Greeks and Troy, a city most likely in modern day Turkey.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The war began when a Trojan, Paris, kidnapped Helen from the Greek King Menelaus.

body: In 1976 the archaeologist Zheng Zhenxiang made an amazing discovery at a dig in eastern China.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: She uncovered a royal tomb, filled with jade, bone and bronze artefacts.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The tomb also contained the bodies of six dogs and sixteen enslaved people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Zhenxiang and her team identified the tomb as belonging to Fu Hao, a queen and general of the Shang Dynasty.

body: The Shang Dynasty began c.1600 BCE in the Yellow River Valley, later than the other major ancient civilisations.

body: Like in Mesopotamia and Egypt, the Shang exploited the fertile land they lived in for extensive agriculture.

body: One reason why we know so much about the Shang Dynasty is because of their use of bronze.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bronze dings were highly important to the Shang Dynasty.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The large size of many dings has led archaeologists to believe they were used to offer sacrifices to gods and ancestors.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If the ancestors of a family were pleased, life for that family would be prosperous.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Dings required complicated moulds to produce. Wealthy Shang Dynasty used them to demonstrate their status.
