title: Pupils may think that sacrifices were only offered to gods.
body: The belief that the ancestors held power over the living family was very strong in the Shang Dynasty. The people wanted to remember them, keep them happy and asked for blessings for their actions in life.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Archaeologists have used the Shang Dynasty's jade artefacts to try to understand their lives.

body: Jade is too hard to be carved and instead must be worn away, taking great skill and patience.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The large number of ornamental jade weapons found suggests how important warfare was to the Shang Dynasty.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Shang Dynasty made many real and imaginary animal figurines out of jade, including the mythical taotie.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some might assume that jade is always green in colour.
body: Jade is a natural stone and so the colour varies greatly. It can appear as many colours including black, brown, yellow, white, green and blue. Different colours have been more desirable at different points in Chinese history.

body: The Shang Dynasty created the first form of Chinese writing in which characters were used to represent words and ideas.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The most detailed examples of this writing exist on oracle bones because they have survived longer than silk or bamboo.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Questions were carved into them and then the bones were heated, causing cracks which diviners would interpret.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Oracle bones were carved with questions about many subjects such as the weather, harvests, and Shang Dynasty rulers.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The oracle bones have provided a wealth of evidence for historians about many aspects of the Shang Dynasty.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1921 an archaeological dig began at a place called Harappa on the banks of the River Indus.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As the archaeologists excavated they began to find evidence of an ancient civilisation in the Indus Valley.

body: About 8,000 years ago the people of the Indus Valley began to farm this land, and got better and better at it.

title: That the civilisation in the Indus Valley began 8000 years ago.
body: Archaeologists believe farming in the valley began around 8000 years ago but the evidence for the cities and civilisation dates from around 5000 years ago.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Following Harappa's discovery in 1921, another major site was excavated in 1922 at Mohenjo-Daro.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They uncovered huge numbers of clay seals, covered in writing and images, along with many pieces of broken pottery.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They also discovered large stone circles on which they think the Indus people threshed their crops.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They also found whistles and figures of dancing women as well as clay toys and figurines.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: From these discoveries archaeologists have worked out that the Indus Valley Civilisation was very large and complex.

title: Pupils may not understand that Britain was formed of separate Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
body: At this time, Britain was formed of four separate kingdoms: East Anglia, Northumbria, Mercia and Wessex.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 870, Wessex was ruled by the young king Aethelred, aided by his younger brother Alfred.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They managed to stall the Viking invasion of Wessex by defeating them at the Battle of Ashdown.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In further battles the Vikings pushed the forces of Wessex back, killing Aethelred in 871.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The new King Alfred fought against the Vikings, now reinforced by the Danish chief Guthrum who had arrived in 872.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alfred made peace with the Vikings, probably bribing them, they went on to conquer Mercia and then Northumbria.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may not realise that the Viking army was so large it was able to split its forces which led to its success across Britain.
body: The Viking army was so large, it could split into different sections and fight in different parts of Britain at the same time. The army could also send reinforcements from one section to support another section in need.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 875 Guthrum began to attack Wessex once again, almost capturing Alfred at Chippenham in January 878.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Alfred raised as many soldiers as possible from across Wessex and defeated Guthrum at the Battle of Edington in May 878.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After the battle Alfred allowed Guthrum to rule the Viking dominated area known as the Danelaw.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Danelaw was north of a line between the Thames to and Mersey, including East Anglia, Northumbria and some of Mercia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As part of the peace agreement Guthrum agreed to convert to Christianity, with Alfred as his godfather.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As the Romans were leaving Britain c.410CE, groups of people called the Angles, Saxons and Jutes began to migrate there.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: These Anglo-Saxons were pagan and polytheistic: they were not Christian.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As they began to dominate Britain, Christianity declined in areas where they settled.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This process was probably helped by the fact that many Britons had not fully embraced Christianity under Roman rule.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For example, at Lullingstone, a pagan shrine built before the chapel was still being used after the chapel was built.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Risking martyrdom, he preached to the kings of north-east Ireland and set up churches.

title: It is widely believed that St Patrick brought Christianity to Ireland.
body: Christianity had reached Ireland through contact with Roman Britain and as a result some Irish people converted to the religion.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By the early 6th century, monasteries began to be set up across Ireland.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At first, these were meant as places for Christians to retreat to and dedicate their lives to God.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were often in remote, hard to reach places like the island of Skellig Michael.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many monasteries, though, attracted the patronage of kings and the rich and grew in both size and importance.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: They were centres for the teaching of poetry, literature, and the arts and produced manuscripts like the Book of Kells.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The strength of Christianity in Ireland led to its own missionary activity, and Irish missionaries travelled widely.

body: Before WWII, healthcare was not run by the government and varied greatly from place to place.

body: Ancient Greece was in the eastern Mediterranean and at its peak spread to other parts of Europe, Africa and Asia.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Greece is mountainous with thousands of islands, leading to many smaller states making up Ancient Greece.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Greek civilisation began c. 900 BCE and lasted until roughly 31 BCE.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 750 BCE, it had colonies in Italy and Sicily but the decline of Ancient Greece coincided with the rise of the Romans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Ancient Greek civilisation developed after the Sumerian, Egyptian, Indus and Shang civilisations.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romans
body: the Romans were a group of people from Italy that took over lots of land across Europe, Africa and the Middle East
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Ancient Greece and Greece are exactly the same place.
body: Modern-day Greece is part of the area that made up Ancient Greece, but it is smaller than Ancient Greece; the extent of the spread of Ancient Greece changed over time.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The land around Athens was hard to farm. Athenians imported lots of food and built a seafaring trading society.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 431 BCE the important city state of Athens was a democracy; Athenians debated and voted on laws in the Assembly.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Men had duties; they had to obey the laws, serve in the army, help run the city, pay taxes and serve on juries.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Women were expected to stay at home and do housework; they cleaned, cooked and wove cloth.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: About 100,000 enslaved people made up about a third of the population and almost every home had at least one.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Athens
body: Athens was one of the largest city-cities in Ancient Greece
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: democracy
body: a system of government in which citizens vote in regular, fair elections for representatives who then make laws and decisions on their behalf
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: assembly
body: a group of components
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: enslaved person
body: a person who has been forced to work without pay, lose their freedom and become the property of another person; sources often refer to them as slaves
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That a country having a democratic government involves all the people in the country having a say.
body: In Ancient Greece, only men were allowed to be part of the Assembly and take part in votes. Women were not allowed to vote, the men made the decisions and the women had to abide by them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sparta was very different to Athens. Sparta conquered nearby Messenia to gain farmland.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Sparta’s government was a council of 30 men: 28 elders who limited the power of two kings, who led the army.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Between 431-404 BCE Sparta fought the Peloponnesian War against Athens to win power over Greece, with Sparta winning.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Women and enslaved people did all the rest of the work; women could own land but could not vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Spartan culture was militaristic; boys left home at an early age to train for the army which they only left aged 60.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Sparta
body: Sparta was a militaristic city in the southern part of Ancient Greece
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: militaristic

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That all city-states in Ancient Greece had the same structure, and the people in each state had the same roles and values. That the city-states were peaceful and lived happily alongside each other.

body: The Greeks had many gods and goddesses and lots of stories and myths that surrounded them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Ancient Greeks believed in 12 major gods and goddesses who lived on Mount Olympus.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Greek Gods were associated with different things, e.g. Hera, Queen of the Gods, was associated with marriage and family.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The popular myth of Persephone and the Underworld shows us how the Ancient Greeks explained the change of the seasons.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Another myth concerned the Moirai, the Fates, which suggests the Ancient Greeks believed in a type of natural order.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a myth is a traditional story, usually about heroes and gods, that is fictional
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, reaching almost 10,000 ft. There were no paths and there was no climbing equipment like we have today. Climbing the rough, rocky terrain was so dangerous it could cost the life of anyone who tried.

body: Ancient Greece was made up of many city-states (polises) like Athens, Sparta and Corinth.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: All the Greek polises spoke the same language and worshipped the same gods; they had a shared culture.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Although all polises were different, they had some similarities such as the agora, a big marketplace.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In each polis, a temple was built at the highest point of the city (the acropolis).
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Each polis also had a gymnasium for men to exercise in, and a theatre where plays were performed.

body: The Bronze Age began nearly 4000 years ago in Britain.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Bronze Age began at different points for different civilisations.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bronze was harder, longer lasting and could be made sharper than wood or stone tools.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This meant that larger areas of wildwood could be cleared for agriculture and more crops could be planted.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This meant that a surplus could be traded or stored in case of disaster.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Populations also grew as the land could support more people, who were needed for increased farming.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Items such as jewellery were often made from gold.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Bronze Age was gradually replaced by the Iron Age in Britain approximately 2800 years ago.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This happened when iron working began to replace bronze manufacture.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Iron is a common metal and is harder and tougher than bronze but harder to smelt as it requires very high temperatures.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the time of this change, much of what is now England was inhabited by the Celtic people who had spread across Europe.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historians are not sure when they came to Britain or whether they did so peacefully.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Celts
body: Celts were groups of people living in Britain and across Europe during the Iron Age
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: a tribe is a group of people, families, or villages that share the same language, customs, and ancestors
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That Celts and Iron Age people were two different things and there was a Celtic Era.
body: Ensure children understand that the Celtic people lived during the Iron Age.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Iron farming tools like the ard plough could be used in heavy clay soils and wetter conditions.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: This allowed a greater variety of crops to be grown, such as oats, and more land to become available for farming.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Iron also allowed the creation of stronger tools, such as axes, meaning further clearing of the wildwood.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With more farming, the number of enclosed settlements grew and land ownership became more important.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Large Iron Age hillforts, like at Castell Henllys and Maiden Castle, were built bigger than any previous settlement.

body: The potter’s wheel arrived in Britain allowing a greater range of quality pottery to be made.

body: Coins were imported to Britain and modified, encouraging trade and shared values for goods.

body: After the Battle of St Albans, Henry VI’s wife, Margaret of Anjou, was determined to preserve her husband’s rule.

body: She ruled on his behalf and built Lancastrian support for Henry, removing Yorkists from court.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Fighting broke out in 1460 with the powerful Earl of Warwick supporting the Yorkists, but York was killed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Edward, York’s son, replaced him and defeated the Yorkists at Mortimer’s Cross and Towton, claiming the throne.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: England had once again been made unstable by arguments over who should be in charge of the country.

title: Students may think the Wars of the Roses ended with the victory of Henry VII at Bosworth and that all historians agree with this interpretation.

title: Victorian women played no political role in Britain in the 19th century.
body: Women were increasingly politically active in Britain, for example, through their involvement in the abolitionist movement and through their participation in trade unions, despite being unable to vote.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1897, Millicent Fawcett set up the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS).
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The NUWSS preferred peaceful means such as writing letters to MPs.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Early campaigns for women's suffrage involved a mixture of middle- and working-class women.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the end of WW2, Britain was in a desperate state, an election was called, leading to a landslide Labour victory.

body: The government was blamed for signing the Armistice, accused of 'stabbing the army in the back'.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Many Germans felt the Treaty of Versailles was harsh and hated the government for agreeing to it.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The treaty forced Germany to pay hefty reparations and give up territory.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Germany's armed forces were significantly reduced and the Rhineland was demilitarised.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dolchstoss
body: the theory that the German army had been ‘stabbed in the back’ and betrayed by Weimar politicians
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: treaty
body: a treaty is a formal agreement between two countries
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diktat
body: an order that must be obeyed, or the act of giving such an order
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reparations
body: payments made by a defeated nation after a war to pay for damages or expenses it caused to another nation
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The belief that the 'stab-in-the-back' theory was based on factual evidence.
body: The theory was a narrative promoted by the military elite to distance themselves from the Armistice surrender. Germany's defeat was primarily due to military exhaustion and economic collapse, not treachery by Weimar politicians.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Weimar Republic faced violent threats from both sides of the political spectrum.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The 1919 Spartacist Uprising, led by communists, sought to establish a workers’ state but was crushed by the Freikorps.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When the Freikorps were ordered to disband they launched a failed attempt to restore the Kaiser: the Kapp Putsch.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The army refused to attack and it was only defeated by a workers' strike.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Assassinations, paramilitary clashes and coups, like Hitler's Munich Putsch, revealed deep divisions in Weimar Germany.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: nationalism
body: the belief that people who share the same language, culture, history or ethnicity should unite in one country; many believe this would create greater unity, strength and harmony within the nation
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: authoritarian
body: authoritarian governments give most power to one leader or a small group, this can bring stability and quick decisions, but offers few rights or choices for ordinary people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: freikorps
body: meaning 'free corps'; a private army formed by ex-soldiers from the First World War
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: paramilitary
body: a group which is organised like an army, but is not official
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Weimar Republic’s reliance on the Freikorps might suggest that the government supported right-wing ideologies.
body: The Weimar Government used the Freikorps out of desperation to suppress left-wing uprisings, but this reliance highlighted its inability to maintain order independently, rather than an alignment with right-wing ideologies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When Germany failed to pay reparations in November 1922, France and Belgium sent troops into the Ruhr Valley.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: German workers were ordered to stop work to prevent the soldiers from taking industrial goods as payment.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Already suffering from inflation, the German economy was harmed by this loss of productivity.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Weimar Government printed money to support striking workers, flooding the economy and triggering hyperinflation.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hyperinflation wiped out middle-class savings, forcing many to barter for survival while others profited from the chaos.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: goods
body: physical resources or products that can be directly harvested or used by people and animals
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: passive resistance
body: the act of showing in a peaceful way that you oppose something, rather than using violence
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inflation
body: a general, continuous increase in prices
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hyperinflation
body: where the price of everything in a national economy goes out of control and increases very quickly
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Hyperinflation affected everyone equally.
body: Some people, like businessmen who hoarded essentials to sell at inflated prices, profited during the crisis. Meanwhile, many middle-class Germans saw their savings wiped out and were forced to barter for survival.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Gustav Stresemann became chancellor during the hyperinflation crisis before becoming foreign minister.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Stresemann ended hyperinflation by taking a number of decisive actions including the introduction of a new currency.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Stresemann agreed two new reparations plans with the Allies: the Dawes and Young Plans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Industrial production and infrastructure were revitalised, reducing unemployment and boosting Germany’s status.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Economic recovery depended on American loans and extended reparations continued to attract criticism of the Republic.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: loans
body: money that is borrowed and has to be paid back, usually with an extra fee
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Rentenmark
body: a temporary currency issued in 1923 to stop hyperinflation
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Dawes Plan
body: an agreement between Germany and the Allies: it restructured reparations, provided US loans to Germany, and led to French troops leaving the Ruhr
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Young Plan
body: an agreement between Germany and the Allies: it reduced Germany’s reparations by 20%, though it faced criticism for prolonging debt
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: infrastructure
body: the basic services and facilities needed for a city to function, such as water supply, electricity, sewage systems, transport and waste collection
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Germany's recovery in the 1920s completely solved its economic problems and secured long-term stability.
body: Much of the recovery depended on American loans. What happens to Germany’s economy if those loans are withdrawn or if the US faces its own crisis? This shows how fragile the recovery really was.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At the end of the First World War, Germany was an international pariah.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the Locarno Pact, Stresemann secured peace by agreeing to respect its western borders with France and Belgium.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Germany joined the League of Nations, restoring its role in global diplomacy and improving relations with prior enemies.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Germany's agreement to the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928 signalled their willingness to avoid conflict in the future.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Stresemann’s diplomacy rebuilt Germany’s reputation abroad, boosting stability and weakening extremism at home.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pariah
body: a person or country who is not accepted by society, especially because they are not liked, respected, or trusted
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diplomacy
body: diplomacy refers to how leaders manage relationships with other rulers and countries; diplomacy can involve making agreements with rulers of other states.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: domestic
body: relating to inside a home or to family relations, this can also refer to existing or occurring inside a particular country; not foreign or international
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was a legally binding agreement that could prevent all future wars.
body: The pact lacked enforcement mechanisms and relied on goodwill, making it more symbolic than practical.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Economic stability under Stresemann improved wages, housing and welfare, but left some Germans struggling.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Housing projects and unemployment insurance improved living standards but strained the Republic's finances.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Women gained greater freedoms and equality, but many still embraced traditional roles at home and in society.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The 'New Woman' symbolised independence and embraced leisure, but some saw this freedom as excessive and irresponsible.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Conservatives viewed women’s new workforce roles and social freedoms as threats to family and national recovery.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Golden Age
body: a Golden Age is a time of peace, prosperity and plenty
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: welfare state
body: a system in which the government accepts responsibility for protecting people's quality of life
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conservatives
body: a group who value tradition, social order and inherited wisdom, wishing to preserve institutions that have stood the test of time, while cautiously allowing for change
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: New Woman
body: a symbol of female independence in 1920s Germany, embracing greater freedom in work, fashion and leisure, while challenging traditional gender roles and societal expectations
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Weimar Republic’s 'Golden Age' benefited all Germans equally.
body: This period brought economic growth, higher wages and social reforms, but not all Germans benefited equally. Many still faced poverty, unemployment and housing struggles. Conservatives also opposed cultural changes, leading to social tensions.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Weimar Germany's 'Golden Age' saw a cultural flourishing and a culture war between modernism and traditionalism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Bauhaus movement revolutionised architecture but critics saw it as an attack on German identity with links to communism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Artists like Otto Dix and George Grosz challenged idealised traditions and depicted social decay.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Berlin’s cabarets and daring nightlife defied authority and social norms, but fuelled a reputation of moral decline.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Weimar cinema pioneered expressionist film, but was later condemned by the Nazis as "degenerate" art.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: culturewar
body: disagreements about cultural and social beliefs between groups, especially between people supporting social change and those against the change
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modernist
body: describes a style or movement, particularly in the arts, that rejects traditional forms in favour of new ways of expression that reflect modern life and ideas
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: degenerate
body: having lost the physical, mental or moral qualities considered normal and desirable; showing evidence of decline
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cabaret
body: a performance of music, singing, dancing or political satire, often held in a bar or nightclub, known for its provocative acts, defiance of social and political norms and embrace of sexual freedom
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Weimar Germany was a completely free and modernist society.
body: While it was a hub of cultural experimentation, it was also deeply divided, with strong conservative resistance and widespread political unrest. Many Germans viewed the cultural changes as dangerous and sought to restore traditional values.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler's belief in Pan-Germanism and antisemitism grew in Vienna; it was later shaped by post-war Germany's instability.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1919, Hitler joined the DAP, which later became the NSDAP promoting nationalism, Volkism and opposition to communism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The 25 Point Programme outlined Nazi core beliefs of reversing Versailles, uniting ethnic Germans and antisemitism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler used his talent for public speaking and propaganda to attract supporters and spread his extremist ideology.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SA was a Nazi paramilitary force that protected meetings, attacked opponents and spread Nazi influence.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pan-Germanism
body: a nationalist idea in which all ethnic Germans or German-speaking people should unite under one German nation
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: socialist
body: a person who believes the government should own key industries to ensure wealth and resources are shared more equally among all people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Völkisch
body: meaning ‘of the people’, it came to be linked to extreme German nationalism and Germanic racial awareness
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: anti-semitic
body: hate or strong dislike of Jews, or actions that express hate or dislike of Jews
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: propaganda
body: propaganda is information, often false, which is published by a person or group to make others agree with them
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Hitler's rise to power was purely due to his use of violence and intimidation.
body: While violence and intimidation played a role, Hitler’s personal appeal was a major factor in attracting support. He was a highly skilled public speaker and capable of delivering passionate speeches that resonated with many Germans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The crises leading up to 1923 created a fertile environment for extremism, making rebellion against Weimar more likely.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Inspired by Mussolini’s ‘March on Rome’, Hitler planned to seize Munich, overthrow Weimar and establish Nazi rule.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The putsch collapsed when Bavarian leaders withdrew support, and Hitler’s 2000-strong march was crushed by armed police.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the short-term, the Nazi Party was banned, Hitler was jailed and many leading Nazis fled.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler gained fame from his trial, wrote ‘My Struggle’ and shifted to a strategy of gaining power legally.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: fascist
body: supports a system based on a very powerful leader, state control and being extremely proud of country and race, and, in which, political opposition is not allowed
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: putsch
body: a sudden and often violent attempt to overthrow a government, usually carried out by a small group
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Bavarian
body: related to Bavaria, a state in southern Germany, which had its own local government based in Munich, the state capital
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'My Struggle'
body: the English translation of 'Mein Kampf', a book written by Hitler while in prison, in which he outlined his life story, political beliefs and plans for Germany’s future
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Munich Putsch was an immediate success, leading to Hitler’s rise to power.
body: The Munich Putsch was a failure in the short-term - Hitler was arrested and the Nazi Party was banned. However, in the long-term, the event gave Hitler national attention and led him to change his strategy, focusing on gaining power legally.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler's ideology, outlined in 'Mein Kampf', reshaped the Nazi Party and later impacted Germany as a whole.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The 1926 Bamberg Conference helped Hitler eliminate socialist elements and solidify his absolute control over the party.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Nazis had limited electoral success as political and economic stability weakened extremism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Nazis gained rural support by appealing to struggling farmers, and shifting focus from urban workers to landowners.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By 1928, the Nazi Party had a national structure, disciplined ideology and tailored propaganda, but lacked mass support.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ideological
body: based on or relating to a particular set of ideas or beliefs
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Führer
body: meaning ‘leader’; a key Nazi idea promoting total authority under one ruler to end chaos, Hitler later adopted it to assert himself as Germany’s supreme ruler
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The 'lean years' meant the Nazis were completely unsuccessful and struggling in every way.
body: The ‘lean years’ mainly refers to the Nazis’ limited electoral success. While they weren’t winning many votes, they were strengthening their organisation, refining propaganda and gaining rural support. These years were crucial for their later rise.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 triggered a global depression, devastating Germany’s economy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: American loans funding German businesses were withdrawn and German industry collapsed leading to mass unemployment.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Weimar government failed to manage the crisis, with Hindenburg using Article 48, fuelling distrust in democracy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Desperation led many unemployed workers to support the Communists, who promised them control over the economy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Fear of communism drove many toward Hitler, and violent clashes between Nazis and Communists escalated.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: depression
body: in this context, a period of economic hardship in which there is very little business activity and not many jobs
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may think that most unemployed Germans turned to communism.
body: While the Communist Party gained support, many Germans, especially the middle class and business owners, feared communism and instead supported the Nazis as a defence against a potential revolution.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Nazi Party gained support as unemployment soared, exploiting economic despair and Weimar democratic failures.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler’s charisma and modern campaign tactics made him appear as Germany’s only hope for stability and power.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Nazi propaganda, led by Goebbels, used rallies, posters, and media to target workers, farmers, and the middle class.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SA used violence and intimidation to silence opponents, with police and courts often favouring the Nazis.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Fear of communism and cultural decline drove many Germans to see Hitler as a necessary protector of Germany.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: propaganda
body: propaganda is information, often false, which is published by a person or group to make others agree with them
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: decadence
body: a state of moral or cultural decline, often associated with excessive indulgence, luxury, or a lack of discipline
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Nazis only gained power through fear and intimidation.
body: In reality, while violence played a role, their rise was also driven by economic despair, propaganda, Hitler’s appeal, and democratic failures. Many Germans voted for them willingly, believing they offered hope and stability.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Reichstag was in deadlock, forcing leaders to rule by emergency decree under Article 48 of the constitution.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Conservative elites removed Brüning and signalled a willingness to work with the Nazis to restore order.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: By July 1932, the Nazis were the largest party, but Hindenburg refused to make Hitler Chancellor, fearing extremism.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hindenburg turned to conservative allies Papen and Schleicher, but both failed as Nazis refused to cooperate.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hindenburg and Papen made Hitler Chancellor, thinking they could control him through a conservative-dominant cabinet.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: deadlock
body: in politics, a deadlock happens when no party or group has a clear majority, so nothing can get passed or decided
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: authoritarian
body: authoritarian governments give most power to one leader or a small group, this can bring stability and quick decisions, but offers few rights or choices for ordinary people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conservative
body: Conservative means very traditional and established - resistant to change.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Franz von Papen
body: a wealthy aristocrat and former army officer; he had little popular support but moved easily in elite political and military circles
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Kurt von Schleicher
body: a senior army officer and political schemer who worked behind the scenes to influence government decisions and shape power from the shadows
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: People “should have known” what Hitler would do once in power.
body: In reality, many elites and citizens saw the Nazis as a lesser evil amid crisis — not as future dictators. The horror of what was to come wasn’t yet clear to them.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler gained power legally but lacked full control and planned new elections to secure a majority.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Reichstag Fire was exploited by Nazis to justify emergency powers and crush political opposition.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With communist members banned and others intimidated by the SA, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Act gave Hitler legal authority to rule by decree, marking his transformation of Germany into a dictatorship.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Gleichschaltung made Germany a one-party state, bringing all areas of life under Nazi control.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dictatorship
body: a dictatorship is another name for a country that is ruled by just one person with absolute power and authority
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Gleichschaltung
body: a Nazi term meaning 'coordination'; the process of bringing all aspects of German life under Nazi control - this meant synchronising all state and social institutions with Nazi ideology
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The Enabling Act was passed fairly.
body: The vote was deeply manipulated: communist Reichstag members were banned, others intimidated.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Röhm’s radical SA posed a threat to the army, business elite, and Nazi Party unity.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler then removed internal Nazi opposition in the SA along with other opponents in the Night of the Long Knives.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler used the SA purge to gain the military’s trust and secure their loyalty.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hindenburg’s death let Hitler merge presidency and chancellorship, becoming Germany’s supreme ruler (Führer).
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A new oath made German soldiers personally loyal to Hitler, not the constitution.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: SA (Sturmabteilung)
body: also known as Stormtroopers or Brownshirts; the Nazi Party’s paramilitary wing who protected meetings and used violence to intimidate opponents
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: socialist
body: a person who believes the government should own key industries to ensure wealth and resources are shared more equally among all people
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: SS (Schutzstaffel)
body: a highly trained elite paramilitary unit, originally formed as Hitler’s bodyguards, later central to Nazi terror and repression
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: purge
body: getting rid of things you don’t agree with can be called a purge
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Führer
body: meaning ‘leader’; a key Nazi idea promoting total authority under one ruler to end chaos, Hitler later adopted it to assert himself as Germany’s supreme ruler
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Hitler was already an all-powerful dictator by 1934.
body: While Hitler had crushed political opposition, the military remained a powerful, independent force. The SA purge was crucial to win over the army, which still had the power to challenge him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Hitler’s regime built a police state using the SS, Gestapo, SD and concentration camps to control the German population.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SS oversaw other Nazi security bodies and controlled policing, intelligence, racial policy and concentration camps.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Gestapo, Germany’s secret police, monitored people, used fear and denunciations to arrest citizens without trial.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles also had a psychological impact of terrifying and dominating the local population.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles were centres of Norman control, acting as bases for Norman nobles to administer an area.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Resentment against Norman rule increased as Anglo-Saxons lost land, money, power and influence.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Eadric the Wild led a revolt against Norman rule in 1067-68.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The most serious challenge to William's rule occurred in the North in 1069.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William’s control of the North was threatened by rebellions.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The resulting famine caused as many as 100 000 people to vanish from the records.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At first, William intended to boost his claim to be the legitimate heir of Edward by keeping earls Edwin, Morcar and Waltheof in place in his government of England - alongside new earls such as Earl Odo of Kent or Earl William of Hereford.

body: The strict conditions for holding land from the king became known as the feudal system.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The feudal system made landholding less secure than it had been under Anglo-Saxon kings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A key relationship in the feudal system was between a vassal and their overlord.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Holding land came with obligations such as paying homage, providing knight service or labour service.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The feudal system increased William’s power and control over England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: fief

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
body: In fact, these promises are with the king and God. It was unlikely you would break a public and spiritual promise like this; it would not have been good for your reputation or your soul!

body: In 1085, William ordered a survey to detail the possessions of his new kingdom of England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Domesday may also have provided William with an accurate account of the tax and soldiers his new kingdom could provide.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Domesday increased William’s royal authority: the capacity to seize and distribute lands, and to charge accordingly.

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Normans made relatively few changes to the English legal system.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Normans introduced the murdrum fine and criminalised the use of resources from royal forests.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)
