body: a Marcher earl was a noble appointed by the king of England to guard the border (known as the Welsh Marches) between England and Wales
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sheriff
body: a sheriff was an official who oversaw law and order in a local area on behalf of the monarch
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: After William the Conqueror was crowned King of England, he and the Normans were immediately accepted as rightful rulers and peace reigned across the kingdom.
body: In fact, William faced a hostile Anglo-Saxon population and threats of invasion from Wales and Scotland, requiring him to take measures to establish further control.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles were almost unknown in Anglo-Saxon England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles had a military function, acting as bases for troops who would control and oppress key areas.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles had a psychological impact of terrifying and dominating the local population.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Castles were centres of Norman power, acting as bases for Norman nobles to administer an area.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most Norman castles were variations of the motte-and-bailey design.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: motte-and-bailey
body: a motte-and-bailey castle is a fortress in which there is a motte (small hill) surrounded by a bailey (courtyard) inside an outer wall
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: burh
body: a burh is an Anglo-Saxon fortification or fortified settlement
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: oppress
body: to treat someone, or a group of people, unfairly
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: keep
body: a keep is the strong main tower of a castle which acted as a watchtower and a final point of defence
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: palisade
body: a palisade is a strong fence made out of solid wooden poles that is used to protect people or a place from being attacked
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A common misconception is that castles only had a military function.
body: Norman castles also acted as administrative centres. They had a psychological function in dominating the landscape and the people who lived there and some castles also helped trade develop.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At first, William wanted to include Anglo-Saxons in the government of his new kingdom, including Edwin and Morcar.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When William reduced their wealth, power and status, Edwin and Morcar rebelled against William.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Edgar Aethling and the Danish king joined the rebellions, which was dangerous for Norman control of the North.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William used different tactics to put down rebellions, one of which was the brutal ‘Harrying of the North’ in 1069-70.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A rebellion in East Anglia 1070-71 saw William repeat his successful tactics to defeat the last Anglo-Saxon rebellion.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: revolt
body: a revolt is when a large number refuse to be controlled or ruled, and take action against authority, often violent action
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harrying
body: harrying is persistently harassing or carrying out attacks on an enemy or an enemy's territory
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: William always used violence to control England.
body: Although violence was a recurring tactic of William's, he also allowed some Anglo-Saxons to keep some of their land and was willing to negotiate and pay the Danes to leave England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William’s control of the North was threatened by rebellions.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William aimed to destroy the spirit of rebellion and ensure that no future rebellion could support itself in the North.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Norman soldiers systematically killed rebels and destroyed food across Yorkshire – later known as ‘Harrying the North’.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The resulting famine caused as many as 100 000 people to vanish from the records.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There were no further uprisings in the North, but William was criticised for excessive brutality.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: systematically
body: when something is done systematically it is done in a way that is done according to an agreed set of methods or organised plan
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: scorched-earth
body: a scorched-earth policy is the act of an army destroying everything in an area such as food, buildings, or equipment that could be useful to an enemy
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: famine
body: a famine is a situation in which there is not enough food for a great number of people, causing illness and death, or a particular period when this happens
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: refugee
body: someone who has successfully sought asylum in another country and is henceforth protected by international law
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: In the medieval period it was expected that rulers would be ruthless in killing anyone who opposed them.
body: Rulers were expected to be just and merciful in the medieval period, and Willian faced criticism across Europe for his brutality in crushing opposition in the North of England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: After the Battle of Hastings, William took the land of all those who had fought against him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: At first William kept some Anglo-Saxons in positions of power to help him be accepted as England’s new king.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The uprisings against Norman rule changed William’s mind about including Anglo-Saxons in positions of power.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William used his control over England’s land to transfer power from Anglo-Saxons to Normans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William’s methods of maintaining control included: military strength, harrying and castles, and government power.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tenants-in-chief
body: tenants-in-chief were the large Norman landholders who held land directly from the monarch
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tenant
body: a person who occupies or looks after property owned by another
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
body: Some Anglo-Saxons, if they had not fought against William at Hastings, were allowed to keep their land.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Three of William’s own earls rebelled against him in 1075, all believing they deserved more land and power.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Waltheof confessed the plot to Lanfranc.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: English and Norman forces cooperated to stop the revolt.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William punished most rebels with prison or banishment, however, Waltheof was executed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The revolt revealed England was tired of resistance and William could rely on Anglo-Norman leadership to secure England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: earldom
body: An earldom was a large area of land ruled by an earl on behalf of the king.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: regent
body: a person appointed to govern a country while the monarch is away or ill
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: garrison
body: A garrison is a group of soldiers that are stationed in a castle.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Resistance to William’s rule of England came only from the English.
body: In 1075, two Norman earls revolted against William, and English forces helped to stop the rebellion.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The strict conditions for holding land from the king became known as the feudal system.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The feudal system made landholding less secure than it had been under Anglo-Saxon kings.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A key relationship in the feudal system was between a vassal and their overlord.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Holding land came with obligations such as paying homage, providing knight service or labour service.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The feudal system increased William’s power and control over England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: feudal
body: feudal describes the old French social hierarchy where the king owned all land and distributed it to those below him, who did the same for those below them, in exchange for work, money or service
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: homage
body: paying homage was to publicly submit and swear an oath of fealty (loyalty) to someone above you in the feudal system
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: overlord
body: an overlord is a person of great power or authority
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vassal
body: a vassal in the feudal system was someone who provided a service (e.g. labour) to an overlord in return for land
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: fief
body: a fief was a parcel of land given by an overlord to a vassal in return for their service to their overlord
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
body: In fact, these promises are with the king and God. It was unlikely you would break a public and spiritual promise like this; it would not have been good for your reputation or your soul!
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The medieval Church was a powerful and influential institution, which William used to spread Norman control in England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William reformed the Church arguing it was in moral decline. It is likely he saw the leadership as a threat to his rule.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most Anglo-Saxon bishops were replaced with Normans, and Lanfranc was appointed as Archbishop of Canterbury.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Lanfranc oversaw a programme of church-building, and bishops were transferred from villages to cities.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Lanfranc’s other reforms included introducing more discipline and a greater separation from non-religious life.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Normanisation
body: Normanisation is the process of making something more similar to or typical of Norman styles, beliefs, customs, etc.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reform
body: to reform something means to change something with a view to making it better
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: simony
body: simony is the buying or selling of advantages or paid positions in the Christian Church, which was considered to be a sin
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pluralism
body: pluralism is the practice of holding more than one religious office at the same time
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Medieval and modern Church power is equivalent.
body: Explicitly outline the Church's organisational power: land ownership, clergy social status, and spiritual authority.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The most significant change in Norman England was the change in the ruling elite.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A positive change was a reduction in the number of enslaved people.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: While some areas were damaged by Norman actions, generally the economy recovered under the Normans.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Anglo-Saxon government systems were sophisticated and the Normans kept much more than they changed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: One area of law that changed significantly was Forest law.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: elite
body: the elite are the group of people who hold power
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: continuity
body: when something continues without changing
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: government
body: a government is a group of leaders who make laws and decisions for a country
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: That the Normans destroyed all Anglo-Saxon government.
body: Anglo-Saxon government systems were sophisticated, perhaps more developed than Normandy’s. The Normans retained and built on the existing Anglo-Saxon governmental institutions.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In 1085, William ordered a survey to detail the possessions of his new kingdom of England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The survey was compiled in 1086, and the two volumes of records became known as Domesday Book.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Historians do not fully agree on the purpose, but Domesday Book gave William a very detailed account of landholding.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Domesday may also have provided William with an accurate account of the tax and soldiers his new kingdom could provide.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Domesday increased William’s royal authority: the capacity to seize and distribute lands, and to charge accordingly.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: survey
body: A survey is a set of questions used to gather information.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: manor
body: a unit of land presided over by a lord
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: geld
body: geld is the name of a tax traditionally used to defend England against (Viking) invasions
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
body: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Norman aristocracy brought with them a distinct warrior culture which included castles and chivalry.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Norman aristocracy viewed their simple and pious culture as superior to the Anglo-Saxon culture.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: English churches were rebuilt in the new Romanesque style that was fashionable amongst the Norman aristocracy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Norman aristocracy spoke Norman-French and used Latin for the Church and official documents.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: aristocracy
body: the aristocracy is a class of people who hold high social rank, often inheriting their status and wealth
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: chivalry
body: chivalry is the system of behaviour followed by knights, that put a high value on bravery, mercy, justice, and generosity
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: piety
body: piety means living in a way that is devoted to religion
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Romanesque
body: the style of building that was fashionable in Western Europe which recalled the power of the Roman Empire
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Penance
body: Penance is a set of actions or a deed done in repentance for sins committed.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: England’s monarchs always spoke English as their first language.
body: In fact, after the Norman conquest it would take over 300 years for the monarch of England to speak English as their first language.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The Norman conquest changed the lives of aristocrats such as Lanfranc and Odo, who in turn impacted England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Odo was made Bishop of Bayeux despite being more focused on secular affairs than spiritual ones.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Odo played an important part in the planning and execution of the Norman invasion of England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Odo was rewarded with land and power; he was made regent, the earl of Kent, and became extraordinarily wealthy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Odo abused his powers, and in 1082, William imprisoned him.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: regent
body: a person appointed to govern a country while the monarch is away or ill
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: secular
body: the opposite of sacred; a part of life that is not to do with the Church or religion
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: According to the Bayeux Tapestry, Odo played an important role in the Norman invasion.
body: There is reason to be sceptical about this depiction. The Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Odo. This perhaps explains why Odo is self-importantly shown as central to the planning and delivery of the invasion.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William had a stern personality, shown in the tension with his eldest son, Robert, (who he nicknamed ‘shorty-pants’).
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Robert believed that William was denying him power, and in 1077, he rebelled.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: William's deathbed succession announcement lacked clarity and divided his kingdom and duchy.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some of the Norman aristocracy agreed that Robert, as the eldest son, deserved to inherit both Normandy and England.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Robert, Bishop Odo of Bayeux, and six of William’s largest landholders launched a failed attempt to remove William II.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: succession
body: the succession is the process of inheriting a title, such as becoming the king or queen
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Realm
body: A realm is a kingdom or empire.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: primogeniture
body: primogeniture is the custom of a family's property going to the oldest son when the father dies
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The one-dimensional view of William as a violent conqueror.
body: In fact, William was very pious and he repented some of the atrocities he had committed during his reign and insisted his treasures should be used to rebuild some of the areas he had harried.
attribution_text: A history lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To make adjectives feminine add -e, change -x to -se, -el to -elle, -en to -enne, -f to -ve, -er to -ère, or no change.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form plural adjectives we add -s, unless the adjective ends in -x or -s. -al and -eau change to -aux and -eaux.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To make comparisons in French we use 'plus ... que', 'moins ... que' and 'aussi ... que' with adjectives and adverbs.

title: To make a comparative adjective in French, add the suffix -er to an adjective.
body: Most comparatives are formed using 'plus ... que' (more ... than), 'moins ... que' (less ... than), and 'aussi ... que' (as ... as). The adjective to compare goes in the middle and agrees with gender and number of the noun being compared.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Present participles can be used as adjectives to describe a noun. e.g. 'une victoire surprenante'.

body: As adjectives, present participles agree in number and gender with the noun they are describing.

body: Some comparative adjective forms are irregular: 'bon' becomes 'meilleur' (better) and 'mauvais' becomes 'pire' (worse).

body: Superlatives describe something as the best, the most or the least e.g: le/la/les + plus/moins + adjective.

body: Some superlative forms are irregular: le/la/les + meilleur(e) (s) = the best; le/la/les + pire(s) = the worst.

title: To make comparatives and superlatives in French, add suffixes -er and -est to adjectives.
body: Suffixes -er and -est do not exist in French. To form comparatives, use the forms 'more', 'less ... than' - 'plus ... que' and 'moins ... que'. To form superlatives, use the forms 'the most', 'the least' - 'le, la, les plus' and 'le, la, les moins'.

body: Present participle adjectives can usefully be combined with other adjectives to give more information about nouns.

body: Comparative and superlative adjectives can be used to enhance opinions and descriptions.

title: The superlative in French always goes before the noun it describes, like in English.
body: Superlatives may go before or after the noun they describe. The rule that applies is BRAGS - if an adjective goes before the noun according to the BRAGS rule, its superlative form will also go before the noun.

body: Most agent nouns follow this rule but there are exceptions, for example 'éduquer' - 'to educate', becomes 'éducateur' - 'educator'. A stem change is needed here.

title: All agent nouns in French end in -eur, e.g. 'joueur'.
body: Many French agent nouns have the '-ateur' ending, for example 'consommateur', which means 'consumer'. This is because these agent nouns are linked to the original Latin forms that French has maintained today.

body: 'Nous' means 'we' when used as a subject pronoun, but it means 'us' when used as a direct object pronoun and '(to) us' when used as an indirect object pronoun.

title: There is only one word in French to translate 'mine', 'yours', 'his', 'hers'.
body: In French, possessive pronouns match the gender and number of the noun they replace in a sentence. They are formed of the definite article and the pronoun, for example: 'les chocolats, ce sont les miens,' meaning 'the chocolates, they are mine'.

title: The preposition 'à' is used to mean 'to' or 'in' for both cities and countries.
body: Prepositions can be tricky to master. Students must practise them carefully and thoroughly. Use 'à' before a city or town. Use 'en' before a feminine country or region. Use 'au' before a masculine country or region and 'aux' before a plural country.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'jouer à' to talk about playing sports and 'jouer de' to talk about playing instruments.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'À' combines with 'le'/'les' to form 'au'/'aux' and 'de' combines with 'le'/'les' to form 'du'/'des.'

body: The 'x' at the end of 'aux' creates liaison before a vowel.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs require 'à' or 'de' before an infinitive, e.g. 'aider à', 'arrêter de'.

title: French indirect object pronouns are all the same as direct object pronouns.

title: There are separate indirect object pronouns in French to replace masculine and feminine nouns.
body: French indirect object pronouns make no distinction for gender (unlike direct object pronouns). 'Lui' means both '(to) him' and '(to) her'. 'Leur' means '(to) them' and can refer to both masculine and feminine nouns.

title: I want to avoid using object pronouns because my writing will be longer and therefore better if I just repeat all the nouns.

title: Past participle agreement only occurs in the perfect tense.

body: Because the passive voice uses 'être', all past participles used must agree in number and gender with the noun subject, including 'avoir' verbs. E.g. La fille est choisie par le réalisateur.

body: Combining the perfect tense and the present tense is a useful way to contrast past and present activities.

title: The [r] sound in German is always the same, regardless of where it appears within the word.

title: I can use 'an' and 'auf' interchangeably to mean 'on' or 'onto'.

title: The only way to communicate about past events in German is by using the 2-verb perfect tense, e.g., 'Ich bin nach Deutschland gefahren. Ich habe dort einen Strandurlaub gemacht.'.
body: We also use the single verb imperfect tense - 'war', 'hatte' and 'es gab', and imperfect modal forms - 'musste', 'konnte', 'wollte', with a 2nd (infinitive) verb, to talk about events in the past.

title: German verbs always stress the same syllable.
body: Generally German infinitive verbs stress the first syllable; however, words starting with inseparable prefixes be-, er-, ge-, ver-, ent- stress the 2nd syllable, which includes most past participles; -ieren verbs stress the 'ie' in present and past.

title: German and English word order are the same.

title: 'You’ in German is just one word.

title: Poetry is always descriptive and doesn't tell stories.
body: Ballads are poems that tell stories with a sequence of events. They include scene-setting, action, change moments and a conclusion. Ballads are also lyrical - they use poetic language, imagery, rhythm, rhyme - and dramatic - often with direct speech.

body: Many two-part separable verbs in German have single word English translations, e.g., 'einkaufen' - 'to shop', 'anfangen' - 'to start'. It is especially important with these verbs not to forget the separable prefix in German.

title: two-verb rule
body: position of the 2nd verb at the end of two-verb sentences, e.g., 'Ich will jetzt Obst essen.'

title: A possessive adjective must match whoever possesses the noun in gender, number and case.
body: A possessive adjective matches the gender, number and case of the noun it describes, not the person possessing it, e.g., 'his school' - 'seine Schule'. The possessor is male but the noun they possess is feminine.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Cardinal numbers (e.g., 'one') are used for counting or quantities. Ordinal numbers (e.g., ‘first’) show order.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Add '-te' to numbers 1-19 and '-ste' to numbers 20 and above to create ordinal numbers, e.g., 'fünfte' ('fifth').
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For dates, use 'am' to say 'on the' and add '-n' to the ordinal number, e.g., 'am fünften August' (on the 5th August).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'in' with the dative case to say 'in' and with the accusative case to mean 'into', e.g., 'ich gehe in die Schule'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Nach' means 'to' with place names and most countries. Use 'zu' plus dative for places with articles, people and events.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cardinal number
body: number form that shows how many of something there are
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ordinal number
body: tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: in
body: preposition which means 'in' with the dative case or 'into' with the accusative case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: nach
body: preposition meaning 'to', used with most countries, place names and places without articles
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: zu
body: word meaning 'to', used with a preceding comma to form two-verb sentences in German that do not involve a modal verb
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Always use 'zu' to mean 'to'.
body: 'To' is expressed in different ways in German. 'In' and 'nach' also mean 'to'. 'Zu' can also mean 'shut', 'closed' or 'off'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: German uses the simple present tense, formed by removing the '-en' from the infinitive and adding verb endings.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Separable verbs are made up of a prefix and a main verb. In the present, the prefix moves to the end of the clause.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In word order three (WO3) clauses, the prefix and verb join up in separable verbs.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Possessive adjectives are used with nouns to show ownership or belonging. They must agree with the noun which follows.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use the possessive adjective 'sein' with masculine or neuter nouns to mean 'its'; use 'ihr' with feminine nouns.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: present tense
body: tells the reader the action is happening now
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: separable verb
body: two-part verb with a prefix and a main verb, e.g. 'aussehen'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All verbs with prefixes are separable.
body: Some prefixes are separable in some verbs but inseparable in others. For example, 'wieder' in 'wiedersehen' is separable, but not in 'wiederholen'. The stress always falls on the separable prefix.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: German uses the perfect tense to describe most past events, but English uses simple past for specific, completed events.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Form the perfect tense with a present tense of 'haben' or 'sein', plus a past participle at the end of the sentence.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Weak verbs form past participles by sandwiching the verb stem with 'ge-' and '-t'. '-ieren' verbs don't add 'ge-'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Strong verbs form past participles with 'ge-' and '-en'. Separable prefixes go before 'ge-'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The order of adverbs in a sentence is time ('um 6 Uhr'), manner ('mit Freunden'), place ('im Haus').
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: perfect tense
body: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: past participle
body: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: time-manner-place (TMP)
body: the order of adverbs in a German sentence - time before manner before place, abbreviated to TMP
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All verbs use the auxiliary verb 'haben' to form the perfect tense.
body: A small number of verbs use the auxiliary verb 'sein' to form the perfect tense. These verbs usually refer to movement or a change of physical state.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pronunciation is important for clear communication. Pay particular attention to the pronunciation of cognates.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form the future tense, use the present tense of werden to mean 'will/going to’ and an infinitive verb at the end.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use a future time phrase with the present tense to mean 'going to' or ‘-ing’, e.g., 'tomorrow I’m doing my homework'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a false friend; 'ich werde' is 'I will'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: werden
body: to become, becoming
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'Ich will' in German means 'I will' in English.
body: 'Ich will' (from the verb 'wollen') means 'I want to', but is a common false friend. The future tense in German needs 'werden' with a 2nd verb in the infinitive.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The vowels [a], [o] and [e] can be pronounced long as in 'gezogen' or short as in 'gewonnen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Strong verbs form past participles by adding 'ge-' and '-en' around the verb stem, e.g. 'gelesen'. Others are irregular.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form a closed question in the perfect tense, swap the position of 'haben' or 'sein' with the subject.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For open questions in the perfect tense, place a question word before 'haben' or 'sein'; the subject follows.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The past participles 'gefallen' and 'gemocht' both mean 'liked'. Use indirect object pronouns with 'gefallen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: past participle
body: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: closed question
body: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: open question
body: question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Questions are formed in the same way in both German and English.
body: English uses 'do you ... ?' or 'are you ... ?' when forming questions. German inverts the position of the subject and verb in a statement to form a closed question. Add a question word at the start to change it into an open question.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use word order one with the conjunctions 'und', 'oder', 'aber', 'denn'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use word order three with the conjunctions 'weil', 'obwohl', 'dass', 'wenn', 'ob', 'da'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use word order two if starting a sentence with something other than the subject, e.g., an adverb.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Possessive adjectives are used before a noun to show ownership or belonging. They agree with the noun they describe.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The genitive case form of possessive adjectives means 'of...', e.g., 'meines Vaters' means 'of my father'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: word order one (WO1)
body: subject - verb - object - the standard word order in a German sentence, e.g., 'ich lerne Deutsch'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: word order two (WO2)
body: inverts the subject and verb in a sentence
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: word order three (WO3)
body: after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: genitive case
body: case used to indicate possession and also used after certain prepositions
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'Denn' triggers word order 3.
body: Not all conjunctions trigger word order 3. 'Denn' means 'because' and is followed by word order 1. 'Weil' also means 'because', but triggers word order 3.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Es gibt' means ‘there is’ and ‘there are’. It is a general statement that something exists.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'da ist' and 'da sind' to point out what there is in a specific place, at a specific moment in time.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Determiners such as 'jed-', 'letzt-' and 'nächst-' change their endings according to gender and case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use dative endings after the preposition 'bei', e.g., 'bei dem (beim) nächsten Mal'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use the correct case after dual-case prepositions such as 'in', 'an', 'auf' to ensure the intended meaning is clear.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'Es ist' means 'there is'.

title: If I don't have a dictionary in an exam, I won't be able to work out the meaning of unfamiliar words.
body: If you cannot use a dictionary, look at the surrounding words. Is the word part of a compound noun? Is it a cognate? Using the words and grammar you know, generate a working translation and try to fill the gap. Consider the topic of the text, too.

title: kein

title: 'Nicht' means 'not' when negating in all German sentences.
body: 'Nicht' negates in many sentences, but 'kein' replaces the indefinite article 'a/an' to negate nouns. For example, 'I have no car', and 'I haven't got a car' are both 'Ich habe kein Auto' in German.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some masculine and neuter nouns add '-er' with an umlaut, where possible, to form the plural.

body: Nouns borrowed from other langauges usually add '-s' to form the plural.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Female person nouns add '-nen' to form the plural.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The German short [a] sounds like the 'a' in 'Blatt'. The short [ä] is as in the plural 'Blätter'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The German short [u] sounds like the 'u' in 'Unterschied'; the long [u] is as in 'Uhr'.

title: plural rule 4
body: add -er to some masculine or neuter nouns, with or without umlaut on a, o, u

title: plural rule 5
body: add -s to nouns borrowed from other languages; for example, 'Interviews'.

title: plural rule 6

title: All German nouns form their plural by adding 's'.
body: Plural rules in German are complex and need to be learnt. Pronunciation is also important, as umlauts [ä], [ö] and [ü] can change meaning; for example, Vater, Väter. Accurate pronounciation can help with vocabulary, reading aloud and transcription.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The SSCs [-ss-] and [-ß-] sound the same.

body: 'Kennen' means to know someone or be familiar with something.

title: [ß] is a capital B and sounds like [b].

body: Word order one conjunctions do not change word order.

title: word order 3
body: (WO3) sends the verb to the end of the sentence or clause after certain conjunctions

title: In German sentences, the word order changes every time you use a conjunction.
body: Word order does not change after common co-ordinating conjunctions. 'Und', 'aber', 'oder', 'denn' just join two standard sentences together. 'Subordinating' conjuctions send the verb to the end of the sentence. Practise with 'weil', 'wenn', 'dass'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use any German infinitive as a noun by nominalising it as a neuter noun.

body: To turn noun-verb phrases to nouns, create compound nouns.

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Verb infinitives only ever mean 'to do' something.
body: Verb infinitives can be 'nouned' or nominalised by capitalising the first letter. These words are 'neuter' and can be used with or without 'das'. They do not need an ending (like the '-ing' in English) and are useful for extending vocabulary.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the future tense with werden plus infinitive and other 2-verb structures.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know that the present tense can be used with a future meaning.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know word order 2 and time before manner before place.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The future tense uses 'werden' in the present tense with a 2nd (infinitive) verb at the end of the sentence.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The present tense with a time adverbial can be used to express future meaning.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Time adverbials modify the time frame for a verb, for example 'this week', 'next month'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 2-verb structures send the 2nd (infinitive) verb to the end of the sentence in WO1 & 2, and to second-last place in WO3.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In reading, use title and picture clues, close reading, translation, and comprehension questions to aid understanding.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: time adverbials
body: adverbs or adverbial phrases which denote time; for example, 'nie', 'schon', 'noch nicht'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: werden
body: to become, becoming

title: 2-verb structure
body: where the 2nd (infinitive) verb comes at the end of 2-verb sentences
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: In the future tense and other 2-verb structures, the 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence.
body: The 2nd (infinitive) verb always comes at the end of the sentence in WO1 and 2. In WO3, where the main verb goes to the end of the sentence, the 2nd (infinitive) verb is in 2nd-last place - 'Ich weiß, dass du nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren wirst.'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When two or more adverbs are in a sentence, the word order is time before manner before place (TMP).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Subject and verb invert in questions and in word order 2, where a sentence starts with a TMP adverb.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Wh- question words focus on time, manner, place, and TMP adverbs can start a sentence in reply.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reading aloud benefits from initial silent rehearsal to focus on the sound-spelling correspondences.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reading aloud also requires focus on cognates with different stress patterns from English.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: time-manner-place (TMP)
body: the order of adverbs in a German sentence - time before manner before place, abbreviated to TMP
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inversion
body: when the subject pronoun and the verb switch place to form a question
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The time-manner-place rule means that all sentences must have time before manner before place.
body: German sentences can start with any adverb to emphasise that element. The TMP order is then retained for any other adverbs in that sentence. For example, 'Mit dem Zug (M) fahren wir morgen (T) nach Liechtenstein (P).'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We use ordinal numbers (e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third') for calendar dates.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form ordinal numbers 1-19 add '-te', e.g., 'fünfte'; for ordinals 20 and over add '-ste', e.g., 'einundzwanzigste'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For 'on the' with dates', use 'am' and add '-n' to the ordinal number, e.g., 'am zweiten März'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For years, separate the digits into two pairs, for century and year, and place 'hundert' or 'tausend' between the pairs.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To infer the meaning of unknown words, examine the surrounding words, review given definitions and select the best fit.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: tells you the order of something, e.g., 'first', 'second', 'third', and is used with dates
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: am
body: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Saying or writing years in German is the same as in English, e.g., 1066 is 'zehn sechsundsechzig'.
body: Block the numbers in pairs as in English, but in German you must use 'hundert' or 'tausend'. 1066 is 'zehnhundertsechsundsechszig'. 2025 is 'zweitausendfünfundzwanzig'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the perfect tense of weak and strong verbs, including the patterns of common changes in spelling of past participle stems.

body: Some verbs have a vowel change in their past participle, such as 'ei' → 'ie', 'ie' → 'o', 'i' → 'u' or 'e' → 'o'.

body: To form a closed question in the perfect tense, swap the position of 'haben' or 'sein' with the subject.

body: For open questions in the perfect tense, place a question word before 'haben' or 'sein'; the subject follows.

title: strong verb (perfect tense)
body: verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: past participle
body: verb form that forms the perfect tense, together with the auxiliary verb
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not change when forming their past participle.
body: Verbs with inseparable prefixes do not add 'ge-' when forming their past participle, but many do have vowel changes, e.g., 'vermeiden' becomes 'vermieden', 'empfehlen' becomes 'empfohlen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun that is the object of the verb and is in the accusative case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: An indirect object pronoun replaces the noun that the verb action is done ‘to’ or ‘for’ and is in the dative case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In sentences with two object nouns, the indirect object noun always comes before the direct object noun.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In sentences with two objects where there is one noun and one pronoun, the pronoun always comes first.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: direct object pronoun
body: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: indirect object pronoun
body: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accusative
body: form(s) used for the object or 'receiver' of the action of the verb
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dative
body: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: When a sentence contains both a direct object and an indirect object, the indirect object always comes first.
body: When a sentence contains both a direct object noun and an indirect object noun, the indirect object always comes first. When a pronoun is used to replace either noun, the pronoun comes first.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Bei' means 'at' or 'with' and takes the dative. When used with masculine or neuter nouns, 'bei dem' becomes 'beim'.

body: Use 'am' as an alternative to 'beim' to mean ‘in the process of’, but only when a single activity is being done.

body: The use of 'beim' or 'am' plus the nominalised verb indicates the activity is, or was, ongoing or unfinished.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In conversation, develop answers by adding opinions and reasons, varying the subject, and adding different time frames.

body: Weak verbs in the present tense follow a regular pattern of changes, like 'lernen'.

body: Strong verbs in the present tense change their vowel in the verb stem in the 'du' and 'er, sie, es' forms.

body: Use reflexive pronouns with reflexive verbs. They often relate the action to the subject of the sentence.

body: Some verbs have the same or similar meanings when used reflexively and non-reflexively, e.g. nennen, to call, sich nennen, to call oneself. However, some verbs completely change their meaning e.g. anziehen, to attract, sich anziehen, to get dressed.

body: Imperative verbs are used to give instructions, directions, or advice.

body: To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak and strong verbs, just remove the pronoun 'ihr'.

body: To use the formal 'Sie' form of the imperative, swap the position of the verb and subject pronoun 'Sie'.

body: 'Sein' is irregular in the 'du' and 'Sie' forms of the imperative. Use 'sei', 'seid' and 'Seien Sie'.

title: Strong verbs follow a different pattern to weak verbs in every person of the verb.

body: The consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the back of the throat and the vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound.

body: An open question is formed by adding a question word before the verb at the start of a closed question.

title: When adapting a question to a different form of 'you', just change the pronoun, e.g., from 'du' to 'Sie'.
body: When adapting a question from 'du' to a different form of you ('ihr' or 'Sie'), it's important to also change the verb form. With strong verbs, this can also involve a stem vowel change e.g., 'isst du?' becomes 'essen Sie?'.

body: To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak and strong verbs, just remove the pronoun 'ihr'.

body: To use the formal 'Sie' form of the imperative, swap the position of the verb and subject pronoun 'Sie'.

body: 'Sein' is irregular in the 'du' and 'Sie' forms of the imperative. Use 'sei', 'seid' and 'Seien Sie'.

title: The word 'laut' always means 'loud' or 'loudly'.
body: As an adjective, 'laut' means 'loud', and as an adverb it means 'loudly'. However, when used as a preposition followed by the dative case, it means 'according to'.

title: Asking yes/no questions in the past is much more complicated than the present tense, as the rules are different. You need to translate 'did'.
body: The English 'did' isn't needed. Swap subject and verb for a yes/no question. 'Er sprach' (imperfect) becomes 'Sprach er?'. In the perfect tense, the past participle stays at the end of the sentence: 'Er hat gesprochen' - 'Hat er gesprochen?'.

title: In a written dictation in German, the only thing that matters is the correct sound-symbol correspondences (SSCs).
body: SSCs are important, but the text needs to make sense grammatically. Check for correct spelling of known words, verb forms and tenses, and singular or plural nouns. Encourage students to check the details and to read back the texts in their head.

title: In German, you always use 'müssen' to say what you have to do.
body: The verb 'sollen' is another way of expressing an obligation, something you have to do. It has several uses, including strong commands (e.g. 'you should ring the doctor straightaway'), which are similar to the 'have to, must' meaning of 'müssen'.

title: When an adjective follows 'ein', always add 'en'.
body: Adjective endings reflect the case and gender of the word they refer to. Dative case adjectives end in -en. In nominative and accusative, use -e for feminine and -es for neuter. Masculine -er and -en match (d)er (nominative) and (d)en (accusative).

title: To say 'it' in German, always use 'es'.
body: As a pronoun, 'es' only replaces a neuter noun. 'Das Buch? Ich lese es gern.' ('A book? I like reading it.'). Use 'ihn' or 'sie' for masculine and feminine nouns. 'Der neue Film? Ich finde ihn (it) toll.'. 'Berlin? Ich besuche sie (it) gern.'.

title: 'Lieber' means 'love'.
body: It is easy to confuse the words 'Liebe', 'liebe' and 'lieber', particularly in spoken German. Pay careful attention to pronunciation and listen out for [er]. 'Liebe' is a noun (love), 'liebe' is a verb (love) and 'lieber' is an adverb (more gladly).

title: Only verbs expressing a change of state take 'sein' in the perfect tense.
body: Verbs referring to motion, which don't require a direct object (e.g., 'gehen'), take 'sein' in the perfect tense. Most verbs meaning 'happen' (e.g., 'geschehen', 'passieren') and the verbs 'bleiben' and 'sein' also use 'sein'.
