title: When producing written work in German, I should stick to short simple sentences.
body: When producing written work in German, you should try to develop and extend your sentences to demonstrate grammatical complexity.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Strong verbs form past participles with 'ge-' and '-en'. Some have a vowel change, such as 'ei' to 'ie' or 'ie' to 'o'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The imperfect tense is usually used in written texts for narration. The perfect tense is much more common in speaking.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The imperfect tense forms ‘hatte’, ‘war’, and ‘es gab’ are often used in spoken as well as written German.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'gerade' with the perfect tense to mean 'just (now)'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'gerade' with the imperfect tense to express that the action was taking place when something else happened.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: perfect tense
body: 2-verb tense that describes completed actions in the past e.g., 'I said', 'she played'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imperfect tense
body: tense used to describe how things were or used to be in the past
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: strong verb (perfect tense)
body: verb whose past participle sandwiches the stem with 'ge-' and ‘-en’ and often changes the stem vowel
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: strong verb (imperfect tense)
body: verb which changes the stem vowel in the imperfect tense, e.g., ‘blieb’
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: gerade
body: adverb meaning 'just (now)'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Always use the imperfect tense to translate the English simple past, e.g., 'I chatted online.'
body: The perfect tense is far more common in German, used for past events in speaking and informal writing. The imperfect is used mainly to narrate past events in more formal writing. However, 'hatte', 'war' and 'es gab' are used in speaking too.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Infinitive verbs can be turned into nouns and correspond to English '-ing' nouns, e.g., 'das Lesen' - 'reading'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To mean 'while' or 'in the process of' doing something, use 'beim' before a nominalised infinitive, e.g., 'beim Lesen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use 'am' as an alternative to 'beim' before a nominalised verb, but only when a single activity is being done.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The use of 'beim' or 'am' plus the nominalised verb indicates the activity is, or was, ongoing or unfinished.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: ‘Deutschrap’ is a form of hip-hop which originates from the 1980s. ‘Rock am Ring’ is a famous music festival in Germany.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: nominalisation
body: the process of making a noun from a verb or adjective
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: infinitive
body: the basic form of the verb, with no particular subject or tense indicated
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bei(m)
body: preposition meaning 'at (the)' or 'with (the)', followed by the dative case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: am
body: preposition meaning 'on the', is a contraction of 'an' and the dative definite article 'dem'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Infinitives and nominalised infinitives look exactly the same.
body: Infinitives can be turned into nouns by capitalising the first letter, so although they sound the same, they look different. They are always neuter. Use surrounding words, such as 'beim' and 'am' to identify nominalised infinitives when listening.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Wenn' means ‘when’, ‘whenever’ or ‘if’, used for repeated actions or conditions in the present or future.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Als' means ‘when’ to refer to a specific past event or point in time. 'Als' and 'wenn' both trigger word order 3.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use the superlative to express the highest degree of something, e.g., 'the most beautiful', 'the best'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form superlatives, add '-st' to the adjective before a noun. Use ‘am’ and add ‘-sten’ to the adjective after a noun.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some adjectives and adverbs have irregular comparative and superlative forms.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wenn
body: conjunction meaning 'if' or 'when' which triggers word order 3
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: als
body: conjunction meaning ‘when’, referring to specific past events, which triggers word order 3
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: word order 3 (WO3)
body: after certain conjunctions, the verb is sent to the end of the sentence or clause
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: superlative
body: a form of adjective or adverb used to express the highest degree of a quality, e.g., 'the tallest', 'the most interesting'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Always use the comparative form of an adjective as the starting point for forming the superlative.
body: Superlatives can change in the same way as comparatives, such as adding an umlaut, (alt, älter, der/die/das älteste). Where the comparative removes ‘e’, use the original adjective to form the superlative (teuer, teurer, der/die/das teuerste).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the present tense in German and its two English translations 'I do' (simple) and 'I am doing' (continuous).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know and can ask verb-subject questions in single verb structures, including reflexive verbs.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know and can ask verb-subject questions in 2-verb structures using modal verbs and werden (future tense.)
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There is just one present tense in German, used to translate the simple present and the present continuous in English.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Imperative verbs are used to give instructions or advice, or to tell someone to do something.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To form the imperative ‘du’ form of weak verbs, remove the ‘st’ ending from the normal present tense form and the 'du'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To make the 'ihr' form of the imperative of weak verbs, just remove the 'ihr'. The verb stays the same.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Verbs with stems ending in ‘-d’ or ‘-t’ add an ‘-e’ to the 'du' form of the imperative.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: simple present
body: verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: present continuous
body: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imperative
body: a mood used to tell somebody to do something or give instructions or commands
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: du
body: subject pronoun meaning ‘you’, informal and singular
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: ihr
body: indirect object pronoun (to/for) her
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: To form the imperative, simply remove the subject pronoun and say the present tense verb form on its own.
body: To use the 'ihr' form of the imperative, simply remove the pronoun 'ihr' and say the verb form, e.g., 'Kommt!'. To use the 'du' form of the imperative, remove the pronoun 'du' but also remove the '-st' verb ending, e.g., 'Komm!'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs are followed by the preposition 'um' and the accusative case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The prefix 'wor-' can be added to 'um' to make a question, usually meaning 'what about' or 'around what'?
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The prefix 'dar-' can be added to 'um' to mean 'about it' or 'around it'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Darum' can also be a conjunction meaning 'therefore' or 'that's why'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Prepositions 'trotz', 'statt', 'während' and 'wegen' are followed by the genitive. Masculine and neuter nouns gain 's'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: preposition
body: word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: da-, dar-
body: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wo-, wor-
body: prefix added to prepositions to form questions
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: genitive
body: case used to indicate possession and after certain prepositions
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'Darum' is a da-compound and its meaning is always directly related to the preposition 'um'.
body: 'Darum' can be used as a da-compund, meaning 'around it' or 'about it' but it is also a conjunction meaning 'therefore' or 'that's why'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A closed question is formed by swapping the position of the verb and subject in a statement.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Add a question word in front of the verb to change a closed question into an open one.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In questions with reflexive verbs, only subject and verb swap position, and the reflexive pronoun follows the subject.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Future or modal (2-verb) questions swap the subject and 1st verb; the infinitive remains at the end.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Varied intonation and accurate pronunciation matter in speaking and reading aloud; punctuation and understanding help.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: closed question
body: question that gets the answer 'yes' or 'no' and is created in Spanish by raising the tone of voice at the end of a statement
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: open question
body: question starting with a wh- word that has more information in the answer than yes/no
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: intonation
body: rise and fall of the voice in speaking
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reflexive
body: describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: modal verb
body: verb of necessity or possibility used with a 2nd verb in infinitive e.g. must, can, want
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Closed questions in German require a translation of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’, as in English.
body: Swap the position of the verb and the subject to create a closed question in German. Do not use translations of ‘do you …’ or ‘are you …’.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know the definite article in the accusative and dative cases, with correct spelling contractions for example 'vom', 'zum'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know singular direct object pronouns
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know some da-compounds, for example 'darauf', dafür, 'damit'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know demonstrative adjectives like 'dies-', 'jed-',and the interrogative adjective 'welch-'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Pupils know some reflexive verbs and the reflexive pronouns 'mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We use direct object pronouns to replace a noun that is the object or 'receiver' of the verb.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Direct object pronouns are: mich-me, dich-you, ihn-him, it, sie-she,it, es-it, uns-us, euch-you, Sie-you and sie-them.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the beginning of a word or syllable and after a consonant.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound after after a long vowel sound, in prefixes -er and -ver, and at the end of words.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: consonantal 'r'
body: pronounced as in 'rot'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vocalic 'r'
body: pronounced as in 'Uhr'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: direct object pronoun
body: replaces the noun receiving the action of the verb e.g. me, you, it, them
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' and object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie' can only refer to people.
body: Subject pronouns 'er' and 'sie' can mean 'he' and 'she' or they can refer to masculine and feminine nouns, meaning 'it'. The same is true for the object pronouns 'ihn' and 'sie', which can mean 'him' and 'her' but also 'it'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some prepositions are always followed by the accusative case: 'durch', 'für', 'ohne', 'gegen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Masculine definite article 'der' changes to 'den' in the accusative case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs are followed by prepositions which take the accusative case.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Verbs which are followed by prepositions often use different prepositions in English.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: preposition
body: word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accusative case
body: used with prepositions to indicate movement towards someone or something
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: definite article
body: the words 'der', 'die', 'das', meaning 'the'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: English verbs followed by prepositions can be directly translated into German.
body: Whilst many of the same verbs are followed by prepositions in both languages, different prepositions are often used, so these must be learnt.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The prefix 'da-' is added to prepositions to refer back to something already mentioned and avoid repetition of the noun.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We use da-compounds for inanimate nouns. We use direct object pronouns for people and animals.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: We use wo-compounds to ask questions with verbs that take prepositions.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Wo' and 'da' become 'wor' and 'dar' before prepositions starting with a vowel.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The consonantal [r] makes a rolling sound at the back of the throat and the vocalic [r] has a gentle ‘ah’ sound.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: consonantal 'r'
body: pronounced as in 'rot'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: vocalic 'r'
body: pronounced as in 'Uhr'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: da-, dar-
body: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wo-, wor-
body: prefix added to prepositions to form questions
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Da-compounds can be used to refer back to any noun already mentioned.
body: Da-compounds can only be used with inanimate nouns. For people and animals, use object pronouns.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To refer back to something inanimate already mentioned, add da- or dar- to the beginning of a preposition.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As a da-compound, 'damit' means ‘with it/them’. As a conjunction, 'damit' means 'so that'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use direct or indirect object pronouns, not da-compounds, to replace animate nouns (people or animals).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Use wo- compounds to ask questions by adding wo- or wor- before the preposition.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: da-, dar-
body: prefix added to prepositions to avoid repetition of the noun
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: object pronoun
body: a pronoun that replaces the object in a sentence
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: conjunction
body: word that connects ideas between clauses in a sentence
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: wo-, wor-
body: prefix added to prepositions to form questions
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: 'Damit' always means 'with it' or 'with them'.
body: 'Damit' has a double identity! It can be used as a conjunction meaning 'so that' as well as a da-compound meaning 'with it' or 'with them'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The indirect object pronouns are 'mir', 'dir, 'ihm', 'ihr', 'einem', 'uns', 'euch', 'Ihnen' and 'ihnen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs, called dative verbs, take indirect objects.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some dative verbs are impersonal verbs.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Bei' means 'at' or 'with'. When used with masculine or neuter nouns, 'bei dem' becomes 'beim'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The biggest ‘Karneval’ celebrations in Germany take place in Cologne.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dative
body: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: indirect object pronoun
body: replaces the person, people or thing(s) that the verb action is done to, when the action is to me, from you, with them; takes the dative case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: bei(m)
body: preposition meaning 'at (the)' or 'with (the)', followed by the dative case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Verbs are only followed by the dative case if we translate the verb with 'to' or 'for' in English.
body: There are several impersonal verbs in German which require the dative case, e.g., 'gelingen' (to succeed).
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The long German [e] can be written 'e', 'eh' or ‘ee’.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Jed-' has different endings in the nominative, accusative and dative cases.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs take indirect objects. They are also called ‘dative verbs’.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: [eu] can be written as 'eu' like in 'neu' and 'äu' like in 'Häuser'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: jed-
body: determiner meaning ‘each, every’ which changes according to gender and case
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dative
body: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All verbs in German are followed by the accusative case, apart from 'sein' which takes the nominative case.
body: A number of verbs are followed by the dative case. These must be learnt and carefully identified when translating into German.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The acronym PALM is useful for describing photos. It stands for People, Action, Location, Mood.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: It is useful to add opinions to personalise photo descriptions.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: There is only one present tense in German. This is important to remember when describing what is happening in a photo.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: simple present
body: verb tense used to express habitual events in the present e.g. 'I do'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: present continuous
body: describes events happening right now: 'I am doing'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The present continuous in German is different to the simple present.
body: The present continuous in German is the same as the simple present, so 'sie essen' means 'they eat' and 'they are eating'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Some verbs are reflexive in German but their English translation does not have a reflexive meaning.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The meaning of a verb can change depending on its reflexive or non-reflexive use.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Reflexive use means the subject (doer) and object (receiver) of the action are the same.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: With plural verbs, reflexive pronouns can also mean 'each other', if the action is reciprocal.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reflexive
body: describes an action where the subject and the object of the verb are the same
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Reciprocal
body: A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of any non-zero number. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal is equal to 1
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Verbs have the same meaning whether they are used reflexively or non-reflexively.
body: Some verbs have the same or similar meanings when used reflexively and non-reflexively, e.g. nennen, to call, sich nennen, to call oneself. However, some verbs completely change their meaning e.g. anziehen, to attract, sich anziehen, to get dressed.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Most reflexive verbs use accusative reflexive pronouns: 'mich', 'dich', 'sich', 'uns', 'euch', 'sich'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If sentences already have an accusative object, the reflexive pronoun must be in the dative.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The dative reflexive pronouns are 'mir', 'dir', 'sich', 'uns', 'euch', 'sich'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The ending of 'welch-' depends on the gender and case of the noun that follows. It follows the same pattern as 'dies-'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: reflexive pronoun
body: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like 'myself' and yourself'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: dative
body: case used for the indirect object in a sentence and after a dative verb or preposition
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: welch-
body: question word 'which'
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: We always use accusative reflexive pronouns ('mich', 'dich', etc.) with reflexive verbs.
body: If there is already an accusative object in the sentence, we use dative reflexive pronouns ('mir', 'dir', etc.) instead, e.g., 'Ich wasche mir die Hände'.

title: Indirect object nouns are always preceded by the words 'to' or 'for' in English, and this tells us we need to use the dative case for the indirect object in German.

body: A direct object pronoun replaces a noun that is the object of the verb and is in the accusative case.

body: An indirect object pronoun replaces the noun that the verb action is done ‘to’ or ‘for’ and is in the dative.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In sentences with two objects that are nouns, the indirect object noun comes before the direct object noun.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In sentences with two objects where there is one noun and one pronoun, the pronoun always comes first.

body: Use 'hätte' to mean ‘would have’, and 'wäre' to mean ‘would be’. No infinitive verb is needed, unlike with 'würde'.

body: 'Sollte' is the conditional form of the modal verb ‘sollen’. It is used to convey what we ‘ought to’ or ‘should’ do.

title: Use 'würde' whenever you want to say 'would'.
body: 'Würde' works in most cases, but for the conditional with 'haben' and 'sein', we usually use 'hätte' ('I would have') and 'wäre' ('I would be').

body: When reading aloud it is helpful to identify and correctly pronounce umlauts, which are common in plural nouns.

body: Cognates are words that have the same meaning and look the same or very similar to English words.

body: Cognates are very useful in reading tasks, as they can help us to quickly identify the overall theme of a text.

title: The present tense in German can only be used to refer to the present.
body: The present tense can also be used with appropriate adverbs of time to refer to the near future, e.g., 'Am Samstag spiele ich Tennis.'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: To talk about what you like in the present tense, use the irregular verb 'mögen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The forms of 'mögen' are: 'ich mag', 'du magst', 'er, sie, es mag', 'wir mögen', 'ihr mögt', 'Sie, sie mögen'.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The conditional form of 'mögen' is 'möcht-' and this is used to talk about what you would like or would like to do.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Möcht-' can be used without a second verb, to express what you would like: for example, in a café or when shopping.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: 'Möcht-' is also commonly used with a second verb in the infinitive to express future wishes.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mögen

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The verb 'mögen' takes regular verb endings.
body: The verb 'mögen' is irregular in the singular present tense forms, and the first and third person singular are identical: 'ich mag', 'er mag'.

body: Cardinal numbers are numbers used for counting or expressing quantity. Ordinal numbers tell us the order of something.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For numbers 13-99, say the 2nd digit first e.g., 'vierundzwanzig' = '24'. For 21-99, add ‘und’ between the two numbers.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For prices, place the € after the numbers and separate euros and cents with a comma. Always say 'Euro' in the singular.
attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: For ordinal numbers, add -te for numbers 1-19 and -ste for 20+. To say 'on' a date, use 'am' and add -n to the number.

body: KaDeWe is short for 'Kaufhaus des Westens' and is a famous large department store in Berlin.

title: cardinal number

attribution_text: A languages lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: German numbers are said in the same way as English numbers, i.e., tens then units.
body: The unit is said before the ten in German, e.g., 'neunundvierzig' = '9 and 40' = 49. It is helpful to write from right to left when taking down numbers so that you produce them in the correct order.

body: 'Welch-' and 'dies-' are very helpful for identifying items when shopping.

title: German question words, like English, do not change their spelling.

body: Infinitive verbs can be turned into nouns and correspond to English '-ing' nouns, e.g., 'das Lesen' - 'reading'.

body: Nouns ending in '-ung' have the equivalent and transparent meaning of the verb, e.g., 'lösen' becomes 'Lösung'.

title: It doesn't matter which Spanish translation of the verb 'to be' we use, as they both mean 'to be, being'.

title: There is only one way to translate the Spanish present tense into English.
body: There are two ways of translating the Spanish present tense into English: the present simple (habit - 'I go') or the present continuous (ongoing action - 'I am going'). The context or time adverbs can help to tell us which one to choose in English.

title: Sometimes parts can be deceptive and look equal but are in fact unequal. For example, the rhombus that has been split into parts with lines that are equally distributed.
body: Explore this further by presenting several examples like this if needed. You could ask the children to try and think of some examples where the parts look equal but are in fact unequal. Getting the children thinking of this will boost understanding.
